In the US, various safety organizations have adopted text-based systems for processing community members' reports of suspicious activities. These organizations receive numerous daily alerts, often lacking context and incorporating personal opinions, leading to informational overload and the risk of missing critical incidents. To mitigate these challenges, we analyzed the system logs from our community safety partner, extracting implicit information from the reports using natural language techniques. Our approach applied distributional semantics to model and identify recurring patterns in report content, as well as key concepts associated with each user based on their previous submissions. Our methods successfully discovered the underlying characteristics of community members' interactions, revealing distinct patterns and themes, and enabling the discovery of previously unseen safety threats and unusual dispatch assignments. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our methods in uncovering hidden patterns, with our evaluation highlighting the challenges and limitations of working with unstructured text data from multiple authors. Our models and analysis are now being utilized to inform the safe and effective assignment of dispatchers to community safety cases. Our work sets a precedent for utilizing text-based data and NLP methods in security and safety domains, and our findings and code are publicly available for reproduction and modification. Additionally, we have developed a dashboard showcasing our models and analysis, allowing users to explore and examine our discoveries in a interactive manner. Our research has also generated new research questions, focusing on extracting explicit information from reports and their sequential patterns, which we plan to investigate further. Our work has already led to an improvement in the overall safety response, reducing the time required to process and assign a safe and effective dispatcher by at least 25%. Our ultimate goal is to develop a comprehensive and predictive profile for each community member, enabling seamless and efficient human-to-human dispatcher assignments and enhancing the overall quality of safety responses. In the long term, our research aims to contribute to the development of intelligent and autonomous systems for community safety. Our work has far-reaching applications and implications, extending to related areas like incident management and emergency response. In particular, our research has significant consequences for the effective assignment of emergency responders, medical teams, and social workers, as well as the accurate prediction of donor-recipient matches and user reviews. To achieve these goals, we will continue to refine our current work and explore new research directions, such as incorporating explicit information from reports, extracting sequential patterns in the data, and utilizing external knowledge to inform our models and analysis. To study the magnetic response of triplet Cooper pairs in a nematic superconductor without spin rotation, we employed the self-consistent Born approximation. Our results show that when a magnetic field is applied at a specific orientation, it induces a magnetic moment, characteristic of Pauli paramagnetism. Furthermore, when the applied field's orientation deviates from this optimal position, the induced magnetic moment decreases due to the counteracting effect of demagnetization. Utilizing a realistic model for Ba$_{0.92}$Sr$_{0.08}$Bi$_2$Te$_3$O$_5$, we calculated the induced magnetic moment in response to varying magnetic field orientations and strength. Our findings demonstrate that within a limited field strength range, the induced magnetic moment behavior aligns with type-I nematic superconductivity, whereas at higher field strengths, it exhibits characteristics of a re-entrant nematic phase. Additionally, our research confirmed that in presence of a weak Zeeman field, the quasiparticle density of states follows a $-\sqrt{B}$ dependence on magnetic field. Our research yields predictions for the magnetic properties of triplets in nematic superconductors, with implications for ongoing experiments. Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods may lead to overfitting if too few labels are provided, while diversity-based methods overlook the model's predictive accuracy. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning framework that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax setting. Our approach incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an adversary that maximizes it, given a limited number of labeled examples. We also develop a practical approximation using a graph-based clustering method, incorporating the classifier's predictions, to achieve efficient computation. Experimental evaluations in image classification and semantic segmentation demonstrate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, particularly when few labels are available. Further details are available in our arXiv preprint: https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.13063. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/jboudric/minimax-active-learning. A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves sequences of random groupings denoted as $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$. These groupings, or partitions $\mathcal{P}_t$, split a continuously increasing set of items $\{1,2,\dots, Rt\}$. When time progresses to $t$, a fixed number of $R$ items are added; we record the occurrence of events associated with each item based on its affiliation to a partition at any given time. It has been proven that, as $t$ approaches infinity, the probability of observing event combinations approaches the sum of independent limits one encounters when following individual items through a reinforcement process, provided those event combinations are feasible given the process's dynamics. Otherwise, the probability remains zero. A particular instance of this process, called the multi-reinforcement process with 'upward' merging, has a notable connection to a renowned percolation model on planar lattices, serving as a suitable proxy for studying the undetermined probabilities of this process. A simulation tool has also been developed to visualize and estimate these undetermined probabilities. Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework. Finally, we explore and establish the equivalent status of the harmony condition for both intuitionistic and classical natural deduction systems. This reveals an unexpected analogy where the harmony condition translates to a form of cut-eliminability in sequent calculus, particularly when cuts are non-complex. This connection offers a novel, proof-theoretic interpretation of cut-elimination as a manifestation of harmonic sequences. This, in turn, reveals cut-elimination as an intrinsic property arising directly from the sequent calculus's structure, rather than being an extrinsic property resulting from a specific proof technique. This provides a further layer of understanding to the notion of harmonic sequences in the Computational Ludics framework. Finally, we derive and demonstrate that the notion of harmony in the Computational Ludics framework can be extended to sequences of cuts in sequent calculus, known as MLL. This reveals an additional layer of understanding to the notion of harmony in the Computational Ludics framework. This, in turn, poses the question as to whether the harmony condition could serve as a generalised notion of harmony for more complex systems such as classical lambda-calculus and classical type theory. We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties. Furthermore, this investigation leads to core-compact equivalents of several core-compact properties in the Smyth powerspace, yet these core-compact equivalents fail to be uniformly continuous mappings. Additionally, we demonstrate that for a large class of uniform spaces, the Smyth powerspace does not have core-compact properties. To address this issue, we develop a new concept - the $\Box$-powerspace - as a refinement of the Smyth powerspace, where the $\Box$-powerspace does uniformly preserve core-compact properties from the original topological space. A crucial aspect of this $\Box$-powerspace is that it is topologically equivalent to the Smyth powerspace when the uniform structure of the original space is upper, but not when it is lower. Lastly, we introduce another concept - the Box powerspace - as a further refinement, which is also topologically equivalent to the Smyth powerspace when it is core-compact, but not necessarily in all cases. This space possesses a more intuitive definition and offers a simpler framework for studying core-compact properties. Moreover, it provides an exact description of the core-compact $\Box$-powerspace when the uniform structure of the original space is upper. We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are embodied in "pointed vortex loops," allowing us to concentrate on their corresponding orbits under area-preserving diffeomorphisms. In the process, we establish a complete set of independent coordinates and demonstrate how an appropriate choice of these coordinates leads to a simple, effective description of the vorticity distribution. Furthermore, we find a general expression for the velocity field and point vortex loop interactions, including those involving a rigid wall. Using these results, we study a few fundamental scattering processes. We also extend our findings to vortex rings and use these results to study certain rigid body motions. Additionally, we demonstrate that certain point vortex loop configurations correspond to hyper-elastic membrane vibrations. Finally, in an appendix, we provide an alternative derivation of our results using a different approach. Although this approach shares many similarities with our main argument, it employs a distinct moduli space formulation. Consequently, most of the detailed analysis is avoided. Nonetheless, we include the appendix in order to showcase this alternative derivation. It is worth noting that the point vortex loop framework has numerous connections with other areas of mathematics, including knot theory and the study of moduli spaces. These connections are not explored in depth here, but they are an intriguing area of research that could be further developed in the future. In particular, we note that certain point vortex loops can be used to construct a Mach number one breaking wave solution to the water wave equations, and this solution is a non-trivial element of the two-fluid Euler equations as a solenoidal vortex. Consequently, this solution belongs to a moduli space that is a direct result of the point vortex loop properties. It remains to be seen what other properties and elements of this moduli space can be constructed. Similarly, although we note in the conclusion that pointed vortex loops may be used to model a variety of physical phenomena, further research is needed in order to fully explore this point. It is worth noting that one particular model which we mention in the conclusion - a pointed vortex loop traveling along a line - has been in use for at least 20 years as a model for animal locomotion. Nonetheless, even though we include this conclusion in order to highlight some of the many connections between pointed vortex loops and other areas of mathematics and physics, the full range of applications remains largely a subject for future research. It is likely that many more areas of research will be influenced by the pointed vortex loop framework in the future

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two steps, initially modeling treatment and outcome to incorporate potential confounders, then applying predictions to ATE estimators, such as AIPW or inverse probability weighting (IPW), often using a parametric or non-parametric framework. Recent advancements in machine learning have led to the development of more sophisticated methods to estimate ATE, particularly with the increased use of neural networks, which can be incorporated into both the modeling and prediction stages. This research focuses on the application of neural networks to the first step and an alternative IPW estimator, typically normalized to handle under-smoothing issues, in the second step. By comparing its performance to other methods such as AIPW, neural network-assisted IPW, and model-conditional expectation, we find that the normalized IPW estimator outperforms others in both realistic data examples and simulations, often achieving accurate results with limited data. Furthermore, this estimator exhibits improved computational efficiency when combined with neural network predictions, making it a viable option when working with large datasets and high-dimensional variables. Finally, we conduct Monte Carlo experiments to examine the asymptotic and finite-sample properties of this estimator, which converge to the true ATE under specified conditions. These results support theoretical conjectures regarding convergence and provide a theoretical foundation for the methods evaluated. Ultimately, we conclude that the normalized IPW estimator with neural network predictions is a reliable and efficient method for estimating ATE, even in cases where the model is misspecified. A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been a staple in the study of baroclinic waves for over five decades, with centuries-old ties to severe atmospheric phenomena.  Despite its prolonged use, research on this setup has waned in recent times.  This study seeks to revive interest in this setup by providing a comprehensive comparison of its performance under various conditions, both in real-world applications and in computer simulations.  By examining the setup's response to different levels of rotation and temperature changes, this study offers a thorough analysis of its behavior under both linear and strong forcing.  The results from the experiments are then matched against those from advanced computer models to gauge their agreement.  What emerged from these comparisons are some fundamental rules governing the baroclinic waves produced by this setup, as well as notable discrepancies between the real-world setup and computer models that require further explanation.  The findings of this study will undoubtedly be instrumental in guiding future research on this classic setup.  Additionally, the relationships between the ages of the researchers involved and the topics explored have been included for extra curiosity.  The study ends on an optimistic note, suggesting that there's still much to uncover in this trusted setup, and that fresh perspectives could still be brought to bear on it. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, its implementation in a Bayesian framework presents challenges, primarily stemming from the connection of extreme value parameters to the rate of a Poisson process. These parameters must be treated as latent variables, whose relationship to the process rate is often unclear in models based on the quantile function. We explore a second class of models, derived from the distribution function, that directly link extreme value parameters to the process rate. These models, however, typically rely on assuming independent and identically distributed underlying variables, which may not be suitable for modelling non-stationary data. We develop a non-stationary model based on the quantile function, specifically for Gaussian distributions, that addresses data exhibiting changes in both the frequency and the most probable value of extreme events. This model ensures continuity of the process and the distribution, and facilitates a straightforward implementation of a Bayesian approach using Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. We demonstrate the performance of this model in simulations and its applicability in real-case studies. In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL. Different from typical robustness in RL, which involves limiting the change in optimal value functions, our study examines the impact of malicious data corruption. Specifically, we investigate an robust offline RL problem where an optimistic MDP is estimated from possibly corrupted datasets in the state and action spaces. To mitigate the effects of corruption, we develop a robust variant of the behavior policy embedding (BPE) framework. Our approach employs the maximum likelihood estimate of behavior policy embedding (MLE-BPE) and incorporates a regularization term to enhance its robustness. We establish a price of robustness and demonstrate the trade-off between robustness and effectiveness in MLE-BPE. Furthermore, we introduce a linear dependence number to evaluate the quality of data and propose the linear dependence regularization (LD-RBPE) method as an alternative to MLE-BPE. We evaluate our approaches experimentally and show their applicability in a variety of settings, including the combination of linear Markov dynamics and action spaces, and the use of deep neural networks. Our methods exhibit superior performance and robustness compared to state-of-the-art baselines in offline RL. Moreover, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approaches in a realistic autonomous driving scenario using the Argoverse dataset. Our code and dataset are publicly available for reproduction of our results. This research is funded by CCF VSSN 2020 Challenge and Award. This research paper is a revised version of the research that was presented at the 2021 IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision. It has been extended with new experimental evaluations and an additional section that examines the robustness of our methods in various levels of corruption. A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with challenge data, underscoring a need for clearer definitions in method comparison. We introduced a new evaluation metric, the average area under the ROC curve across language understanding datasets, which facilitated comparative analysis of the two methods. Our study also highlighted the limitations of current density estimation methods in handling out-of-distribution examples and suggested the integration of language representation learning to improve performance on out-of-distribution examples. In recent years, various artificial molecular motors utilizing electric currents have been explored, and like Brownian machines, they convert electrical energy into mechanical work. Despite their potential to propel individual molecules, these systems are typically modeled as being driven by random electrical force, neglecting the fact that actual tunneling currents can significantly influence the mechanical movement. We have developed a new model for a molecular motor system that takes into account the non-random, force-generating effect of electrical tunneling, considering the tunneling rate and current constant, as well as the hydrodynamic drag on the molecule. This model simulates the dynamical behavior of the molecule, and our results show that its movement is characterized by damped harmonic oscillations. When in motion, the molecule's velocity is proportional to its velocity relative to the solution and the tunneling current it receives, and when it slows down, its deceleration is influenced by hydrodynamic forces. We have derived mathematical equations for the molecule's velocity and acceleration, and our analysis confirms that at equilibrium, it exhibits a bistable behavior, capable of performing macroscopic work in a bistable potential well. We have also found that the correlation between velocity and acceleration is positive, and our model allows for the calculation of the molecule's relaxation time and the tunneling current's influence on its dynamics. These findings agree with experimental observations, and we have demonstrated the generality of our model by applying it to different molecular motor systems. Its predictions also provide a viable path towards building molecular machines that can perform repetitive tasks. Ultimately, our model offers a promising approach to building artificial molecular motors that can efficiently and repeatedly convert electrical energy into mechanical work. Building on a 2014 framework, researchers introduced various interpretations of transducer behavior, some differing significantly from traditional understandings. In this study, further insights into close approximations between two-way and one-way transducer models were gained. Specifically, we demonstrate the possibility of determining whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an equivalent one-way model, with a limit to how complex this transformation can be. Notably, this outcome contradicts traditional transducer equivalences, which were shown to be indeterminable in certain scenarios. We also establish that a similar, more complex equivalence relation for one-way models does not have a solution and, therefore, remains unsolvable. This finding indicates that a 2014 framework for interpreting transducer behavior leads to a greater complexity of equivalence relations compared to traditional transducer models. In a companion paper, we utilize this result to show that a related, more complex model is also unsolvable for determining equivalence. In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$ during the computation of the convolution. Our research focuses on finding efficient algorithms for computing the $n$-dimensional convolution, where each dimension can vary in size $D_i$, under the premise that $f$ is a total function, meaning it is defined and computes a value for every possible input pair from $D \times D$. Our results show that if $f$ is computable in $R(r)$ time, where $r$ represents the size of a portion of one input to the function, the $n$-dimensional convolution can be computed in $n^{O(R(\sqrt{r})\log r)}{R}(r)^{n}$ time. This time complexity significantly surpasses the brute-force approach with an exponential factor, and it remains optimal given the constraints of our problem definition. Furthermore, our study includes a practical application of these findings to improve the efficiency of computing SqueezeBox transformations on binary matrices, a technique used in linear algebra and graph theory operations with the addition of linear constraints. This implementation leads to a substantial reduction in processing time of a graph isomorphism test. Additionally, our algorithm facilitates an approximate $O(\sqrt{n})$ time complexity for a long-standing open issue related to finding the minimum linear sum assignment problem with additional constraints. This research demonstrates that computing general convolution can be a valuable tool in solving diverse problems efficiently. Our algorithms have been successfully tested and validated with the help of additional tools for common problem instances. These experiments not only confirm our theoretical expectations but also demonstrate the practical advantages of our approach, as evidenced by the example code included in this research. This code has also been made available on a public repository for others to access and use. It is worth noting that our results are compatible with a wide range of domains $D$, including integers and binary values, making our findings applicable to a broad range of problems. This research offers efficient solutions to a wide range of issues, including but not limited to, SqueezeBox transformations, graph matching with constraints, finding the minimum linear sum assignment problem with additional constraints, and computing the equilibrium distribution in a game. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, and coughing. To better understand and quantify this risk, numerical models were developed to simulate and analyze the dynamics of aerosolized particles, including a complex model that accounts for the effects of turbulence and a simpler model assuming a uniform mixture. By modeling and reconciling the outputs of these scenarios, our study provides insight into the relative influence of external air currents and human respiratory activities on aerosol dispersion. Our findings suggest that the distribution of aerosol particles is largely determined by their initial generation locations, with the underlying flow patterns playing a secondary role. This outcome implies that predictive models relying on simplified simulations of airflow may be sufficient in predicting the transmission of respiratory diseases, albeit with limitations. Our research contributes to the development of predictive models that could ultimately aid in combating the spread of infectious diseases. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the importance of considering disease transmission within the context of urban mobility networks. Ultimately, our findings present novel perspectives on disease propagation models, encouraging further research in this area. Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work focuses on creating formally verified, executable protocols for double-sided auctions with various requirements, including handling multiple items and quantities of goods, as well as ensuring a fair match with no over-pricing. By applying the Coq proof assistant, we developed these formal specifications and proved their correctness, building on previous studies that introduced unverified double-sided auction protocols for European options. Furthermore, we successfully tested the executable codes within the Coq framework for practical scenarios, such as matching supply and demand of real estate properties and handling auctions of multiple items. The underlying specifications, including for price calculation, have been thoroughly verified to function correctly. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to ensuring the reliability of critical software used in the financial sector. All related materials, including the formal specifications and proof documents, as well as demonstration videos, have been made publicly available on our website. Additionally, the verified codes have been transmitted to an ISLE-based compiler, which then generated executable files for Scala and Java, allowing for functional testing. The timeless appeal of chess persists, with its strategic intricacies still captivating players across the globe, particularly when it comes to mastering the intricacies of Opening Theory which requires extensive knowledge and years of dedicated study. By harnessing the power of large datasets, researchers can now quantify key aspects of chess, including complexity and move similarity patterns in the world of chess openings. This study, the first of its kind to utilize real-world player data, leverages a massive 20 million moves from the online chess community of Lichess, combining this with advanced network analysis and a sophisticated algorithmic approach. Our findings reveal that more complex openings tend to be less popular and exhibit longer histories of usage, whereas similarity in opening strategies is often linked to winning rates, with variations in this correlation observed across different player skill levels. Furthermore, a cluster analysis of opening sets identified distinct groups, allowing for the development of a comprehensive chess opening taxonomy. This work contributes valuable insights to the study of chess dynamics and lays the groundwork for meaningful statistical analysis of this fascinating domain. The collected data and algorithmic approach are openly available for public use, empowering the chess community to gain a deeper understanding of its cherished tactical patterns. Ultimately, this study showcases the immense potential for natural language models to shed new light on complex, human-created domains like chess, where large datasets can be harnessed to reveal intriguing quantitative patterns. Developing free online collections of 3D shapes has driven research in 3D retrieval. Although significant progress has been made, retrieving shapes through sketches in virtual reality remains an area that requires more investigation. Our proposed approach is a virtual reality sketch-based retrieval system for 3D shapes that enables users to manipulate and draw objects in a virtual environment using a headset and controller. Our system can automatically generate complete shapes from these sketches and retrieve similar 3D shapes from a database. To evaluate our approach, we created a virtual reality interface and conducted a study with 30 participants, who achieved an average recall of 50% of the target shapes with our system. Our results demonstrate that sketch-based retrieval in VR outperforms traditional 2D and 3D shaping methods. Our work provides evidence that sketch-based retrieval in VR is a viable and more intuitive solution compared to current techniques. Our system will be open-sourced, allowing researchers to access and build upon our methodology and interface. Additionally, the results and data of our study will be shared to facilitate further research in this area. Our contributions can be utilized by the community in two main ways. Firstly, the generated models can be employed as training data for automatic 3D shape replication algorithms. Secondly, the sketch-based protocol can be adapted and integrated into existing 2D and 3D retrieval challenges to enhance their performance and diversity. Our findings can be further applied to enhance the retrieval of other complex and sketchable objects, such as furniture and buildings. Our research can be expanded to include more advanced features, such as generating sketches from real scenes and integrating image data to improve retrieval results. Additionally, we can investigate the application of neural 3D rendering to create more realistic shapes and scenes, and the utilization of sketch-based retrieval in augmented reality environments. Lastly, we can explore the use of our VR interface to enhance the creative process of 3D designers and artists. Our research can be further divided into three main areas of research, each corresponding to a section in our paper, that can be utilized by the community in the mentioned ways mentioned above. Our contributions are closely tied to the areas of research in neural 3D rendering, sketch-based convergence, and metric learning. Our work is unique due to its integration of these research areas in a VR-based environment, where users can interact and draw 3D shapes through sketches. Our findings provide novel evidence and insights to the research communities of computer vision, graphics, and engineering. Our source code and results will be publicly available for other researchers

This method involves integrating an effective stress tensor and shows, in extension of Wald's formula, that the correction to black hole entropy only depends on the perturbing stress tensor's trace, thereby facilitating a straightforward computational approach. Furthermore, we have found that when the perturbing stress tensor is pure radiation, the correction to extremality bounds and entropy can be accurately calculated analytically. Our approach can be easily adapted for consideration of higher-dimensional black holes. Lastly, in an effort to gain deeper insight into the nature of these corrections, we have performed a detailed numerical analysis on the influence of radiation stress tensor on extremality bounds and entropy in extremal Kerr black holes. This study has further revealed that while corrections become more pronounced as the black hole charge (q/M) increases, they follow an exponential decay in the case of (M/r$_H$)); nonetheless, this increase in q/M is mitigated by the diminution of r$_H$ in comparison to M. Consequently, this behavior has significant implications for the validity of classical extremality bounds in the strong field regime of black holes with substantial charges. In a related context, we have also found that these corrections result in a diminution of black hole entropy compared to its classical value, thereby leading to a corresponding increase in efficiency during the black hole evaporation process. This increase in efficiency has further been numerically quantified and displayed for Kerr black holes under various levels of perturbation. This study has, in extension, shed new light on the long-standing question of how extremality bounds and efficiency are influenced by non-trivial higher multipole moments in black holes. In a final consideration, we have also determined the conditions under which the Iyer-Wald formalism's correction to black hole entropy can be negatively infinite, thereby indicating a critical threshold beyond which the formalism itself becomes invalid. Consequently, this behavior has significant implications for the understanding of black hole evaporation in the context of higher extremality bounds. End-effect models utilize a straightforward statistical representation of policy effects, which serve as a substitute for more complex predictive models. When combined with a reward structure, they facilitate the transformation of a target reward distribution into a feasible policy. However, the initial E-models proposed in the prior work have limitations in capturing correlated effects, which hampers their practical utility in learning intricate motor skills. In this research, we introduce an enhanced representation of effects by incorporating multiple samples of action outcomes, which are then combined using a Gaussian Process to infer the target distribution's underlying correlation structure. We also develop an online method for updating the correlation structure based on the agent's experience. These improvements result in a more robust End-Effect Drive (E-D) algorithm capable of learning complex skills, which is supported by numerical evidence and observations from game simulations. A generalized three-dimensional Poincaré algebra has been developed that incorporates colour symmetry. This enhanced algebra can serve as a basis for modelling coloured Poincaré gravity and exploring generalised models of massive and massless free particles in three dimensions. Multiple generalised particle models have been presented, which distinguish themselves in terms of the coloured Poincaré orbits they describe. Our methodology provides a potential pathway to describing particles in non-abelian backgrounds and serves as a starting point for the worldline formulation of an associated quantum field theory. Furthermore, a classical spinor action has been presented, which features a direct relationship between the curvature of space and the torsion caused by a spinning object, in line with a fundamental principle in generalised coloured Poincaré gravity. This action exhibits a colour-dependent relationship, differing significantly from conventional techniques. Our findings indicate that torsion plays a crucial role in describing coloured particles and spinning particles in an inherently curved space, which has important implications for the description of quarks and other coloured particles in three-dimensional (semi-)conformal quantum field theories. A key characteristic of our coloured Poincaré framework is its ability to describe particles with non-abelian colour charges by implementing colour non-abelian Poincaré algebra constraints on the particle's worldline. This novel approach to coloured particles, with intrinsic charge and spin, in a curved and coloured space, may serve as a valuable tool in various particle and field theory applications. In particular, it enables the precise modelling of quarks in a three-dimensional framework, which has significant implications due to the fact that quarks possess both colour and momentum charges. A fundamental property of our framework is its ability to describe particles with de Sitter Poincaré algebra, which serves as a continuous symmetry, in a curved three-dimensional space. This model distinguishes itself from conventional particle actions by incorporating a finite radius of curvature in space. As a result, our framework may provide a suitable description of particles in curved spaces, which in turn has implications for the development of a quantum field theory from the worldline action. In particular, we expect our model to contribute positively to the ongoing discussions on particle properties in the quantum gravity context. A key feature of our model is its ability to describe particles with an intrinsic spin in a curved and coloured space, which in turn has significant implications for various particle and field theory applications. In particular, it enables the precise modelling of quarks in a three-dimensional framework, which has a crucial role in understanding many phenomena in biology and medicine

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions to effectively solve the upward planarity problem. Additionally, we've derived a fixed-parameter algorithm for the multi-source upward planarity problem, restricted to simple graphs with at most four source vertices. Our proposed algorithms, along with an implementation of the multi-source algorithm, are available online at https://www.ics.uci.edu/~pamirup/UPwardPlanarity.html. Furthermore, we've proved that, in the parameterized sense, deciding whether a directed graph is a subgraph of another directed acyclic graph (DAG) is NP-hard for the number of source vertices parameter. However, we've also found that, in the parameterized sense, deciding DAG-concavity (whether a directed graph is a subgraph of another DAG) is hard to solve, although we've derived a fixed-parameter algorithm based on treewidth. Consequently, we've developed an XP algorithm based on treewidth for identifying whether a directed graph is a DAG. Our proposed algorithms, along with an implementation of the multi-source upward planarity problem, are available online at https://www.ics.uci.edu/~pamirup/DAGconcerned.html. Finally, we've explored the relationship between the DAG-concavity and the complexity of routing problems in directed graphs. Specifically, we've proved that, in the worst case, O(n^k) edges are required in any DAG-r (r≥2) that routes tasks with at least k source vertices. We've also found that, for k=1, such directed graphs (DAG-r) can have at most n-1 edges, and we've derived an XP algorithm based on the number of source vertices for identifying whether a directed graph is a DAG-r. Our proposed algorithms, along with an implementation of the multi-source upward planarity problem, are available online at https://www.ics.uci.edu/~pamirup/DAGr.html. Furthermore, we've explored the relationship between the complexity of routing problems in directed graphs and the DAG-r parameter s, revealing various results and introducing novel fixed-parameter algorithms based on s for identifying whether a directed graph is a DAG-r.

Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to iteratively collect information to reach their objectives.
Previous methods often employ a memory buffer to store encountered images and navigate to the desired goal.
However, these agents typically do not differentiate between the relevance of memorized images to the navigation task.
In this research, we introduce MemoNav, a novel framework that tackles this problem by selecting the most informative memories to visit.
MemoNav relies on a set of diverse memories, obtained by exploring the environment and storing visually distinct images, to guide the agent's navigation.
A novel memory retrieval module then identifies the most relevant memories to visit based on their similarity to the current view and proximity to unvisited areas of the environment.
Through experimentation, MemoNav outperforms existing methods in a simulated outdoor environment and achieves more robust navigation by leveraging a diverse memory library. 
Additionally, the code for MemoNav is available on GitHub for easy reproduction of the results.

This paper summarizes the developments that prompted the need for smaller cells in the past and presents their characteristics. These include advantages such as improved coverage and capacity in hard-to-reach areas, and the ability to optimize resource allocation dynamically. Various deployment scenarios for small cells, such as in outdoor and indoor settings, are discussed, along with their potential deployment densities. Future applications of small cells in the contexts of UDNs, MIMO, AI, and emerging technologies like AR, VR, and LD are discussed. This paper also outlines the key challenges associated with integrating small cells into existing 4G and future 6G wireless systems, and speculates on the potential developments that will shape the future of small cell technology. According to our projections, dense small cell deployments fueled by emerging applications like AR and VR, along with AI-driven and terahertz-based UDNs, will propel humanity towards a new era in human-machine communication. We examine the operator growth in Lie-symmetric systems by generating a large set of bilinear operators in symmetric products and analyzing their correlations. This approach enables us to investigate the entanglement between different modes in quantum field theories, including the free scalar field and $\lambda \Phi^4$ theory, and to compare our results with those obtained from numerical simulations in quantum information. Our analysis focuses on the long-distance and high-energy limits and relates the asymptotic behavior of correlation functions to the rate at which modes occupy larger Hilbert space subspaces. We find that the long-distance behavior of correlation functions is consistent with Gaussian behavior in all cases, but that the high-energy behavior can be non-Gaussian, even in cases where lower-order correlations are Gaussian. In the context of operator growth, this indicates the presence of "super-dense" modes that occupy larger Hilbert space subspaces at higher energies, and we argue that these modes can be understood as super-dense fermionic modes that arise naturally in the $\lambda \Phi^4$ theory due to its fermionization in the high-energy limit. Finally, we suggest that the distinction between Gaussian and non-Gaussian behavior in high-energy correlations could serve as a useful diagnostic for distinguishing between various types of operator growth in quantum field theories. In particular, we argue that the high-energy behavior of correlations in the $\lambda \Phi^4$ theory, in which fermions are present, is more easily understood than that in the free scalar field, in which fermions are not present. In the free scalar field, in contrast, we find that the high-energy behavior of correlations is unpredictable using our methods, and we suggest that the high-energy behavior of correlations in Lie-symmetric systems could serve as a useful probe of the underlying physics of operator growth. In the free scalar field, in particular, we find that the high-energy behavior of correlations is consistent with the hypothesis that the high-energy modes in the free scalar field occupy the entire Hilbert space, and we argue that this behavior could be understood as a consequence of the "fermionization" of the high-energy modes in the free scalar field. The spectator component is almost medium-free and shows a significant 0s orbital component, confirming the expected behavior of this phenomenon. Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds, an external oscillatory instability emerges, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of these intrinsic scales, for a specific crack velocity. Through analytical and numerical investigations, an age-dependent dissipation model is explored, revealing that this oscillatory instability not only persists but also gives rise to a tip-splitting instability under particular conditions, ultimately resulting in multiple cracks along the initial crack line. Contrasting this outcome with the oscillatory instability reveals the importance of intrinsic scales in producing complex behaviors through interplay with other length scales in fracture. The existence of various steady states along a parameter space is demonstrated, allowing for experimental validation and identification of an intrinsic time scale if necessary conditions are met. The internal structure of this fracture phase space map holds valuable information about the physics involved. The critical role of fracture kinetics in fracture instability is underscored, differentiating this concept from patterns seen in other types of 2D material fracture. The findings of this study provide a foundation for understanding fracture instability in 3D systems. The potential applications of these findings in fields such as medicine, geophysics, and materials science are also discussed. The associated code for these numerical studies has been made available.

Historically, the primary focus of communication theory has been on understanding the characteristics of information channels and how to optimize the transmission of information through them. This optimization often relies on the assumption that neither the sender nor receiver has any prior knowledge. However, when the sender has access to additional information about the channel, the problem becomes more complex and there is no single universally effective approach. In contrast, when the sender has access to real-time channel state information, there are established methods such as the water-filling algorithm that allow for near-optimal transmission of information. In this dissertation, we explore two main scenarios - channel state information available with and without feedback - and utilize this information to develop optimal transmission strategies. By utilizing this information, we are able to optimize transmission strategies in both scenarios. In the case where the sender has access to real-time channel state information, we modify the water-filling algorithm to achieve optimal results. Furthermore, when the sender has no access to real-time channel state information but has access to feedback, we employ a predictive approach based on state estimation to achieve near-optimal results. These approaches are validated through numerical simulations and theoretical confirmations. Additionally, we expand upon existing literature by providing a framework that relates these communication problems to control problems, and show that optimal solutions can be achieved with finite computational resources. Finally, we investigate the practicality of these approaches in real-world scenarios. In particular, we demonstrate how the fundamental concepts of this research can be applied to the design of an automatic variable gain amplifier, and successfully verify it through hardware testing. In the context of wireless communication, we demonstrate the effectiveness of these approaches by successfully transmitting wireless signals in an outdoor environment. These research findings are further documented in companion papers. In order to ensure the practicality and real-world applicability of these research findings, we have also conducted extensive experimentation and validation. These experiments involve testing our algorithms on a physical platform, and verifying the results achieved through these experiments with theoretical predictions. These experiments confirm that our algorithms achieve the same results as theoretically expected. In particular, we demonstrate that these algorithms enable near-error-free transmission of information in both directions, and evaluate the performance of these algorithms using metrics such as bit error rate and signal to noise ratio. Furthermore, we investigate the efficiency of these algorithms in achieving high data transfer rates, and demonstrate their resilience to noise through various experiments. These experiments confirm that our algorithms achieve optimal results, and outperform existing algorithms in various metrics. In order to verify the correctness of these algorithms, we have also conducted extensive simulation-based testing.

Additionally, we demonstrate that the spin-orbit coupling interaction can give rise to a nonvanishing chemical potential due to Rashba kinetic energy at the critical value of the coupling constant, which in turn leads to a linear dispersion in the spin-polarized bands at the critical value. Our analysis also reveals that the spin-orbit coupling interaction can protect a topological superconducting phase of the spin-singlet d_x^2-y^2 phase originating from the spin-singlet d_x^2-y^2 Rashba Hubbard model. This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to differentiate between rows that represent a single entity and those that represent collections of entities. To address this, Sem-TAB-Facts, a subtask of the 2021 SemEval Fact Verification and Evidence Finding task, was introduced, with two related goals: interpreting table structures and gathering evidence from these tables to support specific claims. Participants were asked to work on either goal or both, using data in the form of annotated scientific tables. For the table structure interpretation task, human-annotated data were provided, while participants had to annotate their own data for the evidence finding task. A linear model using basic features was employed to simulate human performance for the table structure interpretation subtask, and a transformer model was used for the evidence finding subtask. A linear model, based on logistic regression and character n-grams, was used to evaluate the table structure interpretation subtask, and a similar model, with the addition of wordpiece n-grams, performed best in the evidence finding subtask. To combine scores for both subtasks, a weighted average approach was used. A secondary phase of the competition was also held to compare systems with human annotations as a baseline. Overall, human performance outpaced machine performance in both subtasks. However, it is worth noting that a well-designed model can achieve high accuracy on the table structure interpretation subtask and that a limited dataset for the evidence finding subtask may have limited the effectiveness of a machine-based approach. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. To improve this feedback process, we have developed an innovative testing tool, iTES, which incorporates inquiry-based learning and conceptual feedback into testing. By utilizing iTES, we conducted an empirical study to examine the impact of traditional detailed feedback from existing tools versus the conceptual feedback provided by iTES. The study found that students using iTES showed a 44% increase in correctly identifying test defects and wrote more efficient test codes, as evidenced by a 25% higher code coverage in the final project. Additionally, the study found that students using iTES for all exercises performed better in the final project and had a more stable learning curve than those using traditional tools or only using iTES for the final project. These results suggest that conceptual feedback in software testing education can lead to more direct and efficient learning outcomes. Based on these findings, we propose several theoretical extensions of the feedback mechanism in iTES that can be explored in future research, including the incorporation of conceptual feedback within specific software testing techniques. Furthermore, the study's results can be applied in various educational settings to enhance the effectiveness of software testing training. In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for trustworthy interactions with users. Although various methods for generating explanations have been proposed, few solutions for deep neural networks are both flexible and precise in the sense that they closely mirror the network's behavior. We introduce a novel two-stage approach that integrates concept analysis and integer programming to provide detailed, logical explanations for individual inputs in deep neural networks. By breaking down the decision-making process into distinct components and identifying the relevant variables, our method facilitates the creation of custom, interpretable explanations that capture key interactions between inputs and outputs. We demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing solutions in both accuracy and relevance, offering up to 40% improvement, and impressively, it translates explanations into human-readable form with only 14% deviation from the network's original output. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method efficiently scales for complex networks involving high numbers of variables with minimal impact on computation time. We showcase our solution's effectiveness through practical case studies in social network and image recognition applications. Ultimately, we believe that our innovative method will serve as a pioneering solution for generating precise, interpretable explanations in deep neural networks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/jmgonzalez/CE-DNN.

Achieving single-crystalline layers of rare-earth Heusler films through metal-organic chemical vapor deposition is crucial for their utilization in spintronics and optoelectronics. However, traditional substrate preparation, which involves cutting single-crystalline substrates, is often too expensive for large-scale industrial applications. In this study, the epitaxy of rare-earth Heusler films on graphene/sapphire substrates is explored, with the epitaxial relationship determined by X-ray diffraction and X-ray diffraction reciprocal space mapping. We find that a thin layer of germanium, deposited between the graphene and the sapphire, enhances the quality of the epitaxial films by providing a smooth surface for growth. The growth conditions, such as substrate temperature and deposition rate, are optimized to promote epitaxy, resulting in high-quality films with minimal disorder, as confirmed by a 0.09% strain measured by high-resolution X-ray double-crystal diffractometry. The balanced epitaxial forces responsible for this success are discussed, including remote epitaxy, pinhole epitaxy, and van der Waals epitaxy. The latter is facilitated by a weak van der Waals interaction between the germanium layer and is essential for achieving a low disorder coefficient of 0.003 in the germanium layer, as confirmed by atomic force microscopy. The control of epitaxial forces through the choice of growth conditions and the composition of the germanium layer enables the large-scale production of high-quality rare-earth Heusler films, with a 99% crystalline quality and a 0.09 nm smoothness, for applications in spintronics and photovoltaics. The findings of this study provide a general framework for controlling the balance between remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy and may be applied to other materials to expand our knowledge of epitaxial films. The results of this research could be further developed into a commercial process, enabling the large-scale production of single-crystalline Heusler films for the development of highly efficient spintronic and optoelectronic devices. The study also opens up new possibilities for using graphene as a substrate for growing single-crystalline films, while the produced germanium layers may also find commercial applications due to their high quality and the unique van der Waals properties exhibited. For incorporating large amounts of time series data into other analyses in economics and finance, robust methods are required that can handle non-standard conditions such as heavy-tailed distributions and changes in data characteristics over time.  In this research, we transfer a powerful heavy-tailed multivariate autoregressive model from the field of statistics into economics and finance, incorporating non-stationary trends and diverse distribution patterns while maintaining accurate long-term dependencies.  By employing robust statistical techniques, we establish a framework for estimating a heavy-tailed multivariate model based on observed data and propose an innovative approach for selecting the most appropriate model parameters.  In practical applications, the effectiveness of this model is evaluated through assessments of forecasting, variable selection, and measuring dependence between different data series, in comparison to other available methods.  Notably, our research shows that incorporating long data series into the analysis boosts the model's ability to capture persistent relationships and accurately forecast future data, under both standard and extreme distribution scenarios.  In contrast, the models based on standard statistical assumptions overestimate persistence in data and fail to accurately capture relationships, particularly in the long term, when confronted with complex data characteristics.  In terms of measuring dependence between data series, our research indicates that incorporating long data series into the analysis enhances the model's ability to capture meaningful relationships, under both standard and extreme distribution scenarios, and yields more realistic results compared to other available methods.  Specifically, the models based on standard statistical assumptions underestimate dependence in data, particularly in the long term, and fail to accurately capture relationships, particularly when confronted with complex data characteristics. This study offers the first empirical evaluation of the influence of auction format integrity on bidding tactics and outcome profitability. Through a controlled lab experiment, we investigate whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidders' behavior. Our results indicate that when participants can trust the auction process, they tend to bid more aggressively and reveal their true valuations more frequently. In contrast, bidders in an uncredible environment tend to be more risk-averse and hesitant to reveal their true values. Interestingly, both groups exhibit similar revenue maximization strategies. To further analyze the effects of credibility, we developed an auxiliary game, which we tested in a separate field experiment. Our field findings align with those of the lab study. The significance of this research lies in its potential to improve second-price auction design, potentially leading to enhanced revenue and more accurate price discovery. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between auction design and bidder behavior.

Overall, the BDDC solver emerges as a top choice for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems at high scales. Lastly, the detailed code changes and algorithm modifications outlined in this report are expected to contribute positively to the advancement of cardiac mechanics research in the future. Among these systems are tag-based platforms that enable users to collaborate in annotating shared items such as images and URLs, leading to user-generated metadata pools and collaborative behavior. To unlock this potential, a comprehensive understanding of current systems is required, which involves characterizing these systems based on usage patterns, the evolution of user-generated content over time, and the underlying social dynamics. To address this need, this study conducts an in-depth analysis of 154 existing systems and introduces the ConceptMap, a novel framework for characterizing and comparing these systems based on the features they support. A data set of 35,416 entries is collected through a survey of system administrators and used to investigate usage patterns, measure the extent of interest sharing, and analyze the temporal dynamics of user-generated content. The results reveal both the similarities and differences among these systems and provide a comprehensive characterization that can serve as a benchmark for future research and development in this domain. The findings also highlight the creative solutions employed by the developers to encourage user engagement and collaboration. Additionally, the results shed light on the social dynamics underlying the collaborative creation of user-generated content and reveal the evolution of these dynamics over time. Finally, the study contributes the ConceptMap framework and the resulting data set as open resources for supporting future research and development in this domain. The ConceptMap data set can be accessed at: https://conceptmap.github.io/. The live demo is available at: https://conceptmap.github.io/d3/. The raw data can be accessed via PLOS: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0113198.g001 and https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0113198.g002. The administrators' responses can be accessed at: https://conceptmap.github.io/contacts/. System administrators are invited to regularly update their system's information via this link: https://conceptmap.github.io/update/. The number of existing systems is substantial, which presents both an opportunity and a challenge for uncovering general patterns. The study delves into one aspect of these systems, namely their ability to support collaborative tag-based annotation and the underlying social dynamics, and provides a characterization that can serve as a benchmark for future research and development in this domain. While user-generated content has become ubiquitous in the digital landscape, its collaborative creation is often overlooked, which leads to the social dynamics underlying these systems being poorly understood

Although theoretical frameworks for their design are well-established, practical implementations remain limited, primarily due to the absence of suitable fabrication techniques at ultra-high frequencies. To overcome this challenge, we develop a general strategy for fabricating acoustic metagratings at 1 GHz using two-photon polymerization, and present two successful examples. A detailed analysis of our experiments, compared with numerical simulations, reveals the fine structural details necessary for efficient downshifted acoustic wave transmission. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of our fabrication method by designing a compact acoustic splitter. Our work not only realizes acoustic metagratings at ultra-high frequencies, but also paves the way for widespread application of this technology across a broad frequency range. Additionally, we believe that the techniques described here will contribute substantially to advancing optical metamaterials and metasurfaces. Given the similarities between acoustic and optical systems, this knowledge can be transferred directly. Consequently, we expect our findings to inspire innovative developments in the field of photonics. In this study, we conduct an extensive examination of five leading global optimization algorithms as a hyperparameter configuration problem to understand the overall impact of their settings on performance. By utilizing three methods of sensitivity analysis and evaluating various adjustable parameters, such as covariance matrix adaptation, differential evolution, and non-dominated sorting, we analyze their behavior when influenced by different sampling methods and metrics, providing insights into which settings significantly affect performance and interact with each other. The ranking of influential parameters suggests an optimal order of tuning, and our results also shed light on the overall stability of the algorithms. The presented approach enables researchers to identify critical settings for further investigation and facilitates the development of targeted adjustments, as shown in the observed improvements when optimizing hyperparameters. The accompanying open-source software allows for replication of the study's results and provides pre-optimized parameter configurations for quick integration into existing projects. Furthermore, we outline potential future applications and contributions of this research, including the exploration of complementary analysis techniques and the extension of this study to the optimization of problem-specific parameters. Ultimately, the proposed methodology could promote the development of more robust and efficient evolutionary algorithms by prioritizing the optimization of critical hyperparameters. The source code for replicating the study's results is publicly available at https://github.com/jbrc-optimization/gsa-eva.eyJ.

It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is analogous to certain relationships between charge, current, and the wave equations. The paper then demonstrates that these relationships lead to quantised electromagnetic field energy displaying the characteristics of the Balmer series. Finally, the paper discusses the connection between its developments and Bohr's atomic model. Although the paper attempts to provide a self-contained derivation of the Balmer series, it is essentially building on earlier work by Dirac, discussed in the concluding chapter of his monograph, and a series of papers by Jaynes, as summarised in a more recent article. This derivation employs the wave equations and the non-radiative condition in a manner similar to Bohr, but using the charge and current distribution instead of atomic orbits. Furthermore, the paper's developments are expressed in terms of the four-potential, A, and four-current, J, in a manner consistent with the Lorentz gauge, as recommended by Dirac. The paper explores the implications of its findings on the fundamental status of quantum theory, and whether these developments could lead to a quantum theory purely of the wave equation type. Ultimately, the paper concludes that its results and suggestions raise more questions than they answer, and that further research is required to address these concerns and possibilities. In the realm of lifelong reinforcement learning, specialists utilize their knowledge to improve more complex tasks, integrating data from various environments.  The challenges of this area can be broken down into several key obstacles:  the ability to transition between distinct tasks, the ability to learn multiple tasks, and the ability to apply knowledge across different environments.  The lack of comprehensive frameworks limiting evaluations to specific aspects, such as state representation and experience sharing, characterizes existing lifelong learning solutions.  A new framework, L2Explorer, is introduced to address the void in comprehensive evaluation methods for lifelong reinforcement learning.  It offers a series of interconnected tasks in a realistic setting, along with a system that automatically adjusts training and assessment processes.  The primary connection of the tasks is based on the similarity of their requirements, and the platform allows experts to focus on specific skills, using predefined training settings and tools to support their development.  A set of baseline models, well-established in standard reinforcement learning, are also utilized to measure the practical value of lifelong learning methods.  The effectiveness of one lifelong reinforcement learning strategy, also serving as a benchmark, is evaluated using data collected from L2Explorer in an unsupervised training process.  The results show a notable improvement in the practicality of this method after being trained using the platform's data.  The code for L2Explorer, as well as the collected data and the experiments' settings, are available for use, promoting collaborative research in the field of lifelong reinforcement learning.  The platform is intended to facilitate collaborative research in this area, encouraging contributions in the form of published papers.  A call for contributions is also issued, inviting experts to develop their models utilizing L2Explorer, and the collected information will be regularly updated on a dedicated webpage. Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. However, Liger's data complexity necessitates a customized data processing system to refine its output in real-time, making it compatible with science data reduction software. This processing system, called the Data Reduction System, will be responsible for delivering science-ready data to astronomers and coordinating observations with the adaptive optics system. We have outlined a comprehensive plan for the data processing pipeline and defined the interfaces between subsystems, as well as the protocols for data exchange with external libraries and software packages. Furthermore, we have established clear guidelines and constraints for data formatting and encoding to ensure interoperability with other observatory tools and data repositories. This processing system will maintain full transparency by maintaining publicly available code and documentation, ensuring that data remains openly accessible to Liger scientists and observers. This paper provides a detailed overview of the data processing strategy for Liger and serves as a reference for the design of the Data Reduction System, its interfaces, and protocols. It is anticipated that this design will contribute to the development of next-generation data processing systems for future ground-based astronomical instruments. Keck Liger Data Reduction System notes are publicly available at https://github.com/kligerdrs/kliger-drs-docs for community review and feedback. This document will be regularly updated as the project progresses at https://kligerdrs.github.io/. Keywords: Liger, data processing, infrared devices, exoplanets, stellar physics, astrometry, photometry. This study uncovers a broad class of non-trivial and smooth travelling waves that arise in the vicinity of the Couette flow in 2D Euler equation, at low regularity in vorticity. The distance from the Couette flow is measured by the vorticity field's L2 distance, and it's shown that as vorticity decreases, the distance from the Couette flow exhibits asymptotic stability, supported by a robust estimate. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this asymptotic stability is robust against small disturbances in both the velocity and the vorticity fields. The proof involves constructing a nonlinear correction mechanism and establishing a self-contained and fully nonlinear model for the disturbance's evolution, which is linked to a Hamiltonian system with conserved properties, allowing us to achieve geometric decay towards Couette flow. This approach offers a more flexible framework that could be applied in other situations where Euler equations exhibit similar characteristics. Interestingly, we discover that the limit we approach as vorticity vanishes does not align with Geonno and Masmoudi's and Zhang's rough estimates, which instead converge to a unique profile that dominates the behavior of the vorticity, and is shielded by a novel barrier function that provides an alternative approach to Masmoudi and Zhang's conjugate system. The study also reveals that without assuming zonal symmetry, a broad class of non-trivial and smooth travelling waves can still be identified, which are linked to a rough change in energy that remains open for further exploration. Lastly, we show that an analogous result can be achieved in the context of the 2D Euler equation with a constant background flow. Due to the novel mechanisms developed here, this study significantly expands upon Masmoudi and Mieyan's results, which only considered smooth travelling waves. Masmoudi and Mieyan's results were published in a preprint of the same title in 2020. Our results reveal a unique combination of anisotropic trapping potential and Planar Concave Inner Mirror (PCIM) effects that amplifies polarization-dependent anisotropy. The anisotropy is observed in both single and coupled condensates, and is quantified through the analysis of macroscopically occupied single-particle spectral line shapes and polarization-resolved optical microscopy images. The anisotropy reverses when the axis of the trap is rotated by 90 degrees, and the system spontaneously reverses its polarization without external influence. Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. Under a slightly modified constraint - that the sumset A plus a single-element subset of B doesn't exceed 2k - it's proven that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. Furthermore, it's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every five-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions with a bias. Lastly, it's speculated that this generalised 5k-5 theorem should apply equally to finite abelian groups.

X-ray images of COVID-19 patients contain subtle characteristics that can predict patient outcomes. Our research investigates how to identify these subtle features in X-ray images that are indicative of the severity of the disease in hospitalized patients, with a particular focus on factors that contribute to critical illness. By analyzing image patterns, we aim to determine which imaging features have the potential to predict which patients are at higher risk of developing critical symptoms and need immediate intensive care. This study aligns with the goals of the SIH2021 challenge, which seeks to identify ICU admission features in X-ray images, and our findings complement the challenge's objectives by exploring potential details within these images. Through thorough experimentation, we established that models can accurately classify patients for ICU admission based on aggregate characteristics, but our analysis also uncovers potential details within these images that could further enhance predictive capabilities for critical symptoms in COVID-19 patients. These potential details were previously overlooked in the context of the SIH2021 challenge. Additionally, our research highlights the diverse set of potential features in X-ray images, which vary widely across different datasets, and emphasizes the need for thorough data collection in line with clinical standards. Our code and models will be publicly available to enable replication and verification of our results. Furthermore, our research provides a foundation for future studies to investigate whether subtle image patterns have predictive value for patient outcomes in COVID-19, beyond ICU admission, and can guide clinical decisions with image data in clinical settings. These decisions can also inform medical professionals whether pulmonary symptoms in COVID-19 patients are progressing towards critical symptoms as seen in ICU treatment. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the potential of image-based predictive models to facilitate rapid and effective decision-making in clinical settings, particularly when complemented by expert medical judgment. Additionally, our research underscores the significance of image data in understanding disease progression and understanding patient outcomes in a real-world setting. Finally, our research underscores the value of machine learning models in understanding and analyzing image patterns and their relevance to predictive capabilities in medical image recognition. These findings can also be applied in non-supervised and self-supervised learning models to predict critical symptoms in COVID-19 patients. These models were previously overlooked in the context of the SIH2021 challenge. Our research provides a foundation for future studies to investigate these models in clinical settings.
