We analyze the transmission eigenvalue problem for the Helmholtz equation in spherically layered media, considering the case where media properties exhibit step changes or continuous variations. Our research demonstrates that boundary localization of transmission eigenfunctions is possible under all scenarios, and we provide specific conditions and examples to illustrate this phenomenon. Furthermore, our findings show that transmission eigenfunctions with distinct radial phases can coexist near a boundary, whereas in the medium's interior or exterior, such functions display radial phase consistency. This study confirms that transmission eigenfunctions can effectively act as sensors, probing a medium's boundaries and properties of inhomogeneities. Our analysis also highlights the relationship between boundary localization and phase transitions in transmission eigenfunctions. Finally, we anticipate that our findings will contribute to the development of novel computational methods for transmission eigenvalue problems. These results stem from recent works by Liu and Su [J Math Anal Appl, 505(1), 2021], and Yang et al. [J Differential Equations, 287, 2021]. Our work presents a comprehensive exploration of boundary localization, encompassing all possible scenarios of layered media, and provides a unified understanding of this phenomenon. Optimized hardware is a critical consideration in embedded systems, where code efficiency directly affects performance and energy consumption. Repeated operations in digital signal processing (DSP) codes can be accelerated with a single unit, but also require additional components, ultimately influencing the overall cost. Existing research often prioritizes code size over hardware requirements or vice versa, without accounting for the actual costs associated with embedded circuits. This work addresses the neglected area of optimal hardware efficiency in DSP codes, proposing a novel framework that generates DSP codes with the lowest hardware requirements, rather than just the most compact code. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods in terms of hardware efficiency while still maintaining optimized code size. Furthermore, we have found that the optimal hardware efficiency can be closely related to the minimum number of multiply-accumulate operations required in some cases. Our framework is versatile and can be adapted for other efficient unit considerations with modified objective functions. Our experiments show that the optimal multiply-accumulate count can be attained within a factor of $3.35$ of the minimum achievable value, indicating that our framework provides near-optimal hardware efficiency. We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the essence of nonterminating processes in a compatible manner, we employ the option type, thereby generating a model that is compatible with the original Scott model developed in the context of lattice theory. Our analysis specifically focuses on the ordered type theory NP, and we demonstrate that the developed model maintains the requisite properties of a Scott domain, including positivity and the lack of chain infinite bounds, wherein the former requires an intricate application of univalence. Furthermore, we thoroughly investigate the properties of the model, and through a series of forcing theorems, we show that the denotational and operational semantics of NP are in equivalence, thereby providing a formal proof that the two semantics are equal. This achievement represents a significant outcome, as it formally establishes the equivalence of the constructive and classical Scott semantics in a predicative and reductivist setting. Lastly, we formally derive a constructive version of Tarski's fixed point theorem for NP. The entire formalization is implemented using the Coq proof assistant and is made publicly available. Moreover, the associated documentation provides an in-depth overview of the formalization, alongside a comprehensive guide on the interpolation property, a critical concept that plays a pivotal role in the analysis but lacks a formalized treatment in the existing literature. Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$. 
The resulting expression is then related to an Eisenstein series from $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ 
constructed using the Speh representation $\Delta(\tau,n)$. 
This new approach avoids the reliance on specific character properties as in earlier methods. 
Instead, the general strategy of Hanzer and Muić is utilized, 
pathway relying heavily on the manipulation and analysis of linear characters and their connections to characters of $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$. 
Ultimately, the cancellation of poles is tied back to an expression involving characters of $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$, specifically characters derived from the symplectic double cover and its connections to a specific character of a torus in $SO(2n+1,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$. 
Key concepts include the utilization of a specific Hecke algebra and character relation, a concept developed by Asaora-Kano. 
Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the expression of a certain character of $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ can be broken down into the combination of a character of a torus in $SO(2n+1,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ and an expression tied to a linear character of $GL(1,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$. 
Ultimately, the outcome shows that the cancellation of a specific Eisenstein series from $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ can be described through a character of a torus in $SO(2n+1,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ and an expression tied to a linear character of $GL(1,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$.

Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure. Traditional control approaches rooted in geometric control may struggle to adapt to changes in the robot's geometry obtained from real-world sensing data. To address this, we develop a novel control framework that leverages sensing data to create a mobile robot's geometric blueprint and safely navigates it around obstacles. Our method incorporates a Control Barrier Function that dynamically adjusts its collision avoidance strategy in line with the robot's changing geometry, while also factoring in its instantaneous velocity. To facilitate the integration of sensing data, we develop an innovative system identification technique that enables the translation of sensor readings into the robot's precise geometric representation. Discrete-time Control Barrier Function, paired with a Sequential Least Squares Polynomial Algorithm, works in tandem to create a compact and reliable representation of the robot's spatial structure, thus empowering safe navigation even in complex environments. Our approach has been successfully tested and validated through real-world experiments using a Turtlebot mobile robotic platform connected to a Digits robotic arm. These experiments, conducted in simulated and real-world environments, showcase the efficacy of our method in generating practical and safe control inputs for the robots. Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity. An experimental framework is established to evaluate the efficacy of distinct graph-based approaches and their combinations, all of which aim to identify the most pertinent sentences to include in a summary. Our study showcases the advantages of a hybrid approach consisting of Graph-based Ranking Pont (GRPT) and Leadness, which surpasses a conventional system in terms of accuracy. Furthermore, our findings reveal that a strategy built upon the analysis of sentence sets (token overlap) outperforms its counterpart based on individual sentences (word overlap). Ultimately, our proposed solution outperforms the leading machine learning-based model in the TSAR challenge and rivals the top-performing human contributors. Our source code is freely accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/aman2810/TSAR-Challenge. Additionally, the pre-trained models can be obtained from Hugging Face's model hub at https://huggingface.co/aman2810. We eagerly look forward to your feedback and suggestions on improving this work. We believe that making our code and models publicly available will facilitate replication of our results and foster collaborative research efforts. In particular, we believe that our approach to text summarization using graphs can be adapted to resolve various challenges in named entity recognition, dependency parsing, and part-of-speech tagging, and may find applications in diverse areas such as question answering, sentiment analysis, and text classification. We envision the potential of our graph-based method to serve as a fundamental building block in natural language processing tasks. Researchers have suggested the application of quantum interferometry and information processing in Bose-Einstein condensates. However, the current understanding of BECs relies on complex descriptions, often through quantum field theory or nonlinear differential equations. These descriptions sometimes conflict with key principles in interferometry and processing, such as linearity. Nevertheless, exceptions can occur, particularly when interferometry and processing are implemented in closed systems with confined photons. This study builds upon this exception, transferring knowledge from nonlinear scalar photons to a BEC context. We develop a quantum gate, a fundamental tool in interferometry and processing, and demonstrate its application in a BEC setting. The gate's structure, derived from the soliton's conservation laws, reflects the symmetries inherent in the BEC's Gross-Pitaevskii equation. The gate's efficiency also connects to the soliton's stability, recently studied in the context of Bose condensates of massless and massive magnons. The gate's implementation, achievable through laser manipulation, offers a novel pathway to controlling light and its nonlinear counterpart in the BEC context. The gate's properties, replete with intriguing phenomena such as entanglement, dark states, and revivals, provide a rich framework for exploring quantum optics and related fields associated with BECs. The study's findings also suggest possible applications in magnonics and quantum computing systems using magnons and cavities. The intersection of interferometry and processing, exemplified through our quantum gate, provides a unique platform for advancing these fields through the unique perspective offered by BECs and nonlinear photons. The platform also warrants a exploration of bootstrapping approaches to controllable quantum mechanics. The study's contributions transcend BECs, as they offer novel insights into nonlinear optics, magnonics, and quantum computing, expanded by the intriguing possibilities opened up by the nonlinear gates in the BEC context. The research also suggests an interesting connection with similar issues in black hole physics, particularly those related to the feedback mechanism and the amplified reflection property of nonlinear gates. The same principles could potentially be applied to the self-dual solitons in a particular type of black hole solution, the smart holes, for which a similar quantum gate could be defined. The study's findings may also find applications in Bose condensates of phonons and in quantum computing systems based on cavities. The research offers an original perspective on quantum information processing, as it extends the nonlinear gates' properties to the unique context provided by the BECs and, by extension, to nonlinear photons and magnons. Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained using ideal-theoretic techniques like saturation ideals and equidimensional decompositions. We propose an algorithm leveraging signature-based features of Gröbner basis algorithms to directly calculate the Gröbner basis for the nondegenerate locus ideal directly. This method avoids the need to find saturated ideals and equidimensional decompositions through an interactive process involving user input and algebraic analysis. The algorithm's implementation is incorporated into the Mathematica package GrBasis. The computational efficacy of this method is demonstrated with a range of examples, which also highlight its limitations along with potential enhancements. The underlying algorithmic concepts are further explained with a detailed theoretical section. The study concludes by addressing potential avenues for further research and development. The observed direct photon yield in this study is similar to that found in Au$+$Au collisions at the same energy, and significantly lower than predictions made by various theoretical models for most central Au$+$Au collisions. The measured direct photon yield in Cu$+$Cu collisions is about 15\% of the predicted quark-gluon plasma suppression in most central Au$+$Au collisions at the same energy. The observed suppression of direct photons in Cu$+$Cu collisions is comparable to that found in Au$+$Au collisions and suggests that the Cu$+$Cu collision system also experiences a form of quark-gluon plasma. The relative suppression of quarks and photons in Cu$+$Cu collisions is similar to that found in Au$+$Au collisions, and indicates that the quark-gluon plasma in Cu$+$Cu collisions is as abundant as in Au$+$Au collisions. Furthermore, the measured direct photon yield in this study is lower than predictions made by various theoretical models for a system that lacks a quark-gluon plasma, and indicates that the quark-gluon plasma in Cu$+$Cu collisions is thicker than in Au$+$Au collisions. The thickness of the quark-gluon plasma in Cu$+$Cu collisions is less than that in Au$+$Au collisions when the momentum transfer is low. The measured direct photon yield in this study is higher than predictions made by various theoretical models for a system that lacks a quark-gluon plasma when the momentum transfer is low. The difference in the direct photon yields in Cu$+$Cu and Au$+$Au collisions at the same energy is a manifestation of the finite size of the nuclei used in these experiments. Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos offer valuable insights into pulsar wind properties, the diffusion of particles in supernova remnant shocks, and the galactic gamma-ray background. This review focuses on the galactic pulsar halos, presenting statistical data on their numbers, luminosities, and spectral indices, as well as spatial characteristics. Pulsar halos are rare, accounting for approximately 5% of all pulsar wind nebulae. They are identified as having extended gamma-ray emission at high frequencies and large sizes, often exceeding 0.1 deg in radius, with total energy exceeding 10^47 ergs. Most pulsar halos originate from young pulsars, aged less than 3.5 ky, and are found in supernova remnant systems, particularly those with large sizes and advanced ages. Research on pulsar halos has contributed to an understanding of particle acceleration in supernova remnant shocks, as evidenced by the sharp cutoff of a pulsar halo's light curve, emitted by particles outside the shock. Studies on very high energy gamma-rays from a few pulsar halos, such as PSR B1259-59, confirm that a substantial portion of emission originates from a large-scale halo. to common weather conditions in the US and lack more rare or unusual weather
scenarios found in other parts of the world, such as heavy fog common in Europe.

in international settings. In response, a new, comprehensive dataset has been created

for extensive manual labeling of data. The proposed dataset and corresponding code
are both accessible for free use by the research community. Evaluations of various

all weather conditions, outperforming other baseline models substantially. Evaluation
results also demonstrate TransWeather's ability to accurately classify rare weather
scenarios with a moderate error rate of 10\%. Furthermore, a detailed study of
error distributions provides valuable insights, shedding light on the challenges posed
by specific weather conditions and potentially informing future research in weather
classification. To summarize, a new, comprehensive weather classification dataset is
presented along with a proposed architecture, named TransWeather, and associated code
and dataset are all freely accessible for use at the linked website.

Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions. Ultimately, our findings suggest that policy decisions in the climate change domain would benefit from considering scientific evidence more closely.

A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra, specifically via measurements of the density power spectrum. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial synthetic dataset of absorption spectra and associated density maps is generated in the vicinity of a large number of quasars. A series of machine learning models is developed to reverse-engineer this data to estimate the underlying density distribution from the spectra. This inverse estimation process yields a fitted density map for each quasar, and a series of tests using mock datasets reveals that the models can accurately predict the underlying density distribution at a precision of about 10% on large scales. A subsequent analysis using over 3000 synthetic quasars demonstrates that the models can estimate the underlying density distribution with a precision of around 20% at a depth of about 200 thousand kilometers. Notably, the models perform best when the signal-to-noise ratio of the reconstructed density maps matches the range found in the training dataset. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs, but developing a scalable dialogue system for real-world use remains challenging due to the diversity of roles within a conversation. To effectively build a dialogue system, it is crucial to identify and label a dialogue role, yet current research lacks a standardized approach for role specification. To address this issue, our work defines a role as a set of essential utterance characteristics, including the presentation of information, as demonstrated in existing human-human conversations. We developed a pipeline to create a role-specification dictionary and used it to design a data-driven dialogue system that learns to generate responses based on roles. By leveraging large-scale language models and annotated data, our system demonstrates promising results, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in open-domain dialogue tasks and showcasing the efficacy of role-guided dialogue systems. The proposed methodology and developed dataset are made available for the community to explore and improve role-specification in open-domain dialogue systems. A thorough approach is outlined to simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. The proposed methodology acknowledges the fractures as distinct entities, meshing the fractures and the porous matrix separately with high-quality quadrilateral meshes. The fundamental conservation principles are discretized by a coherent MDMD method, resulting in an accurate and conservative numerical scheme. A series of numerical experiments demonstrate the capabilities of this approach, including tests on individual fractures, isolated fracture domains, and more complex fracture networks. The results showcase the efficacy of this model in simulating a wide range of fracture geometries and domain configurations. Furthermore, comparisons with existing 3D DFRM models reveal good agreement between the proposed methodology and other methods, validating its implementation and accuracy. Lastly, simulations of solute transport in a complex fracture network validate the quality of the numerical solution and the underlying model equations. These experiments serve as a fundamental foundation for future three-dimensional fracture network simulations. Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and the vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered high-quality. To enhance article quality, we focus on identifying and improving unreliable articles citing low-quality sources. By analyzing editing behaviors, we developed an automatic labeling system for identifying articles written poorly and thus of low quality. This method utilizes machine learning and predictive analytics to assess patterns in user behavior associated with low-quality articles. In our tests using a Wikipedia dataset of 2.8 million articles and 5.2 million revisions, we achieved an accuracy of 80% in identifying low-quality articles and 70% in identifying reliable articles. Compared to existing methods, our approach is more efficient, requiring less manual labeling, and more adaptable, as it can be applied to newly created articles without additional labeling. We also found that articles requiring significant editorial work are more likely to be of low quality, and that our system can accurately identify articles needing such revisions. Finally, we demonstrate that our approach can be used to automatically label low-quality articles in Wikipedia's latest version with minimal retraining. The implementation of this method has already improved the accuracy of Wikipedia's quality metrics and can be applied to other collaborative projects with relevant editing logs. Typically, this process relies on the teacher model being accessible and its internal workings being understandable, which is not the case in black-box settings. In contrast, decision-based models can operate in the data-free and label-free regimes, but the process of training them is often complicated by the difficulty in formulating a suitable loss function. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable agents' actions. Experimentation across various scenarios highlights the potential of CoIL to surpass traditional reinforcement learning performance, demonstrating promising applications. A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods. This novel approach enables researchers to model and understand treatment interference within connected networks. At the core of this method lies a statistical test called the Standardized Difference of Observed Treatments (SDOT), which consistently shows the lowest type I error rates and the highest statistical power across various scenarios. Furthermore, the chosen strategy for selecting focal units consistently outperforms other methods in maintaining type I error rates and detecting interference. As a result, the proposed approach serves as a reliable and efficient means of detecting treatment interference within connected networks. Related material is available online.

To address these limitations, this study proposes an SRAM-based TRNG that exploits the statistical properties of bitflips in SRAM arrays to generate random numbers. The proposed TRNG incorporates a novel technique that under scales the SRAM supply voltage and leverages the SRAM's read operation to extract entropy from the most sensitive bits. To validate the design's reliability, numerous tests were performed, generating over 1 billion random bits. The experimental results show that the proposed TRNG exceeds the NIST requirements for a high-quality random number generator. What's more, the design offers enhanced robustness, a reduced implementation burden, and increased flexibility. The design's performance outperforms the current best SRAM-based TRNGs in these areas. Consequently, the proposed TRNG can be integrated into various applications as a reliable and high-quality TRNG. The properties of thin films made of metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate the electronic properties and fluctuations of monolayers of SrMnO$_3$ and CaVO$_3$ using a cluster-embedding method. Our results show that, in contrast to experiments, the mean-field approximation predicts no finite-size effects. However, by reapplying the self-energy corrections to the embedded orbitals, we find large fluctuations in the films. Our results are validated by comparing them with density-functional and quantum Monte Carlo calculations. We estimate that films with a thickness of four layers or more can be considered bulk-like, and our findings suggest that recent observations of negative magnetoresistance in strained SrMnO$_3$ films can be explained by orbital fluctuations. Furthermore, we conclude that electron correlation in these films is driven by orbital fluctuations rather than spin fluctuations. In the case of CaVO$_3$ monolayers, we find that antiferromagnetic ordering is unstable against ferromagnetic perturbations, indicating that magnetism may not be stable in this system. Our results suggest that magnetism in ultrathin films requires careful consideration of surface effects. Finally, we note that our results provide a framework for understanding the magnetism in LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ heterostructures. Our findings can be applied to other systems to identify the relative importance of spin, orbital, and electronic fluctuations. Additionally, our results imply that surface state mediation could be a universal feature of oxide heterostructures with potential applications in spintronics and quantum computing. Furthermore, we propose that these materials could be used to demonstrate the quantum Eraser experiment to test the principles of quantum mechanics. Finally, we note that our results provide a new paradigm for the design and understanding of magnetism in transition-metal oxides. Conversely, our findings also provide new avenues for the design and understanding of superconductors, as we identify a new class of superconducting compounds and provide new insights into their operation at the quantum level. A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice. With this method, the Wilson coefficients are constrained at the 0.1% level, and the fit is largely insensitive to hadronic parameters and $BR$-related issues affecting standard analyses. This new method is expected to play a crucial role in the precise determination of the $C_9$ Wilson coefficient and the effective dipole moment in the Wilson coefficient $C_9$ with the full data from the LHCb experiment at its current sensitivity level. The formation of these condensations involves a cooling process, but they can also be destroyed by nearby hot IC components through a heating-to-cooling imbalance. To study the growth and disappearance of these condensations, we employed two-dimensional numerical simulations that incorporated adaptive mesh refinement within a 2 x 10^15 K temperature range. The simulations included realistic galaxy cluster density distributions, a realistic ICM alpha factor, anisotropic magnetic field lines, thermal conduction, and a sophisticated radiative cooling model that can pass through heavy elements. The results show that magnetic fields strongly impact condensation dynamics, with head-on collisions causing condensations to dissipate. However, when magnetic fields are oriented at an angle, they fail to shatter the condensations, allowing them to survive and potentially form large structures, ultimately contributing to the development of large-scale radio halo phenomena. The results also validate previous findings that thermal conduction leads to a homogeneous ICM state, but with conductance reduced by a factor of 100 or more to mimic a "non-equilibrium" state. The study suggests that magnetic field lines must be tightly tied to thermal conduction for an equilibrium to occur. The results also show that cold condensations can grow under specific conditions, ultimately mirroring the large-scale structures of radio halo emissions observed in galaxy clusters. The study lays the groundwork for a new "shatter-and-grow" mechanism that could explain the origin of these large-scale radio halo phenomena. Additionally, the results emphasize the need for further galaxy evolution studies that incorporate magnetic field processes to accurately model galaxy cluster observations. The examination of $C$ and $CP$ violation in beauty- and charm-hadron decays serves as a crucial element in assessing the standard model's precision and its capacity to predict naturally occurring phenomena. The discovery of direct $CP$ violation in 2001 marked a significant breakthrough, followed by the finding of $CP$ violation in charm hadrons in 2011. The investigation of $C$ and $CP$ violation in these processes is ongoing. The presentation outlines the latest findings from the LHCb, Belle, and Belle II experiments, focusing on the areas of $C$ and $CP$ violation in beauty- and charm hadron decays. The discussion includes insights into the distinct roles of mixing and direct $CP$ violation in beauty hadrons, the latest analysis involving data from run I and II of the LHC, and an examination of the potential for $C$ and $CP$ violation in exclusive charm decays. The material covered represents input for the spring 2022 Particle Physics Review. The review also touches on the LHCb's plans to study rare exclusive decays of beauty hadrons and $CP$ violation in these processes, in addition to discussing prospects for $C$ and $CP$ violation research related to the Higgs boson and light leptons. The LHCb is expected to achieve $33$ times more data by the end of run III, which will significantly enhance statistical precision and open up fresh avenues for exploration. The potential for further breakthroughs in the field, particularly concerning rare exclusive decays and $CP$ violation in these processes, appears promising. The LHCb's forthcoming goals and strategies were also discussed. The creation of Belle II's integrated luminosity will reach $20$ times its initial value by the end of its data-taking period, which is anticipated to occur at High Energy Accelerator Research Organization (KEK) in 2027. The assessment of $CP$ violation in beauty hadron decays at Belle II and the LHCb will likely lead to highly precise results, which will significantly test the standard model's predictions. The standard model anticipates no $CP$ violation in most charm hadron decays, whereas numerous rare exclusive decay processes of beauty hadrons that are not influenced by $CP$ violation are being actively studied. The potential for discovering new physics beyond the standard model's scope exists in these analyses. The LHCb's forthcoming goals and strategies were also discussed. The material covered in this review represents the latest findings and plans

We have developed new bounds on the minimum success probability of a quantum state transformation within the probabilistic framework. These bounds can be expressed as an optimal value over a specific type of matrix norm, which can be further linked to the relative entropy between the target and resource states. As a key finding, we derived a critical threshold for the relative entropy that guarantees a successful transformation within a finite number of trials, while also estimating the required number of trials needed to achieve a given success probability. These results generalize previous findings on deterministic state transformations, revealing a trade-off between the success probability and the number of trials needed to confirm the target state. Furthermore, we applied our general approach to establish new bounds on the entanglement manipulation cost, a measure of the minimum number of entanglement erasures required to transform a given quantum state into another. By analyzing the geometric properties of the Bloch matrix, we showed that the entanglement manipulation cost can be bounded by a quantity proportional to the relative entropy between the target and resource states, which is a more accurate estimate than previously known bounds. Additionally, we found that the entanglement manipulation cost achieves its maximum value when the target state is a maximally entangled state, thereby establishing a critical threshold for the relative entropy that must not be exceeded if a fully entangled state is to remain so. We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot shifted horizontally due to external excitation, causing the parameters to change in the vertical plane. The resulting motion was analyzed for specific parameter settings, with particular focus on stability and limit cycles, using numerical methods and the largest Lyapunov exponent. The results show that certain combinations of parameter values lead to stable and unstable behaviors, in comparison to a statically supported pendulum. We also observed an analogy between our findings and a carnival ride, noting that the most enjoyable experience for passengers occurs under specific conditions. The relationship between excitation frequency and angular displacement was mapped and the occurrence of a jump discontinuity was numerically determined. The work presented here is a tribute to the late Michael Grimes, a colleague and friend who inspired this study with his "grinding" idea. The findings can be utilized to explain why sipping coffee is generally considered a bad habit. We also identified a phenomenon dubbed "sloshing," which enables our model to capture the essential physical characteristics of the system and provides valuable insights for designing optimized transportation methods. Furthermore, our research facilitates a deeper understanding of a pumped pendulum and expands the knowledge base of nonlinear dynamics. The study offers a comprehensive examination of a ground-level problem, demonstrating how complex dynamics can emerge from seemingly simple everyday activities. The investigation also sheds light on the connection between the movement of a carried cup of coffee and the angular displacement of a pumped nonlinear pendulum. We demonstrated that the dynamic behavior of both systems can be accurately represented and simultaneously analyzed. Lastly, our research clearly illustrates the link between the sloshing motion and the grinding of coffee that initiated this study, solidifying the relationship between physical parameters and mathematical abstractions. We concluded that both the physical system and the mathematical model exhibit identical behaviors, with the latter effectively capturing the essential features of the former. The study provides a thorough examination of a ground-level problem that arises from the everyday movement of a car. We also discovered new and unexpected aspects of both the physical and mathematical systems under consideration, leading to novel general observations and outcomes. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD. Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we mathematically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of O(1/K) and even better performance under unknown data distribution scenarios, reaching a rate of O(1/\sqrt{K}). Furthermore, we conduct comprehensive numerical experiments to demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms current state-of-the-art decentralized optimization methods by a significant margin. Additionally, we apply our proposed algorithm to a real-world use case, specifically a robust speech recognition task in a decentralized network setting. The results show the efficacy of our approach in effectively handling data distribution changes and performing robust optimization in such networks. We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma. Since the hydrodynamic response is the same for all collisions with the same centrality, any deviation from this universal behavior indicates additional particle production mechanisms that are specific to each collision. Therefore, by analyzing collisions with low multiplicities of produced particles, our research predicts the presence of enhanced particle production mechanisms resulting from the fragmentation of the initial state, whereas at higher multiplicities, this effect diminishes and is overshadowed by the collective response of the quark-gluon plasma. Furthermore, we investigate how the characteristics of the initial state impact the collective behavior observed in high-energy collisions and identify specific instances where initial-state effects could manifest. Lastly, building upon our research, we propose a method to determine the non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma by analyzing the differences in produced particle numbers between nucleus-nucleus and proton-proton collisions, which occur under the same conditions but result from distinct initial energy states. This novel approach reveals that the non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma are more pronounced than previously acknowledged, accounting for a significant portion of the collective behavior observed in high-energy collisions and illustrating the profound impact of the initial energy state on the collective behavior of the quark-gluon plasma. Lastly, our research also addresses questions regarding how quickly the quark-gluon plasma achieves equilibrium by analyzing the relationships between produced particle numbers, initial energy states, and energy release in nucleus-nucleus collisions at various collision energies. Factors such as the object's size, material, and solar distance, influenced by the radiation pressure parameter Q/b, contribute to these predictions. A linear difference equation modeling the objects' motion allows for the identification of resonant locations and boundaries, while numerical modeling based on Lissajous orbits helps to visualize and refine these regions. Additionally, we examine the impact of eccentric orbits on these resonances. Extensive numerical simulations, spanning a period of 10,000 years for various parameters and under different conditions, provide further insight into objects' behavior. A key outcome of this research is a graphic representation illustrating the stability of objects at resonant locations in relation to their orbital characteristics. This work ultimately contributes to a diagram representing the layout of these resonances and providing critical information for predicting the trajectories of objects influenced by solar radiation pressure. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models using quantum information concepts, particularly unitary design techniques.  By employing these ideas, we create precise and controllable tight-binding models that accurately replicate complex quantum systems while maintaining exact physical properties, such as the electronic band structure, despite the influence of light.  Furthermore, we demonstrate the development of a method to generate arbitrary Hamiltonians with high accuracy while ensuring the overall system remains in the correct physical framework.  This method is highly versatile and can be applied to produce an expansive variety of Hamiltonians on any given network.  Ultimately, we show that it is possible to construct tight-binding models that simulate complex quantum systems while maintaining exact physical properties and accurately replicating the influence of light.

Our comprehensive approach considers both two-dimensional and three-dimensional semantic keypoints for object interpretation, and we thoroughly evaluate our methodology by applying it to real-world autonomous vehicle datasets, such as KITTI and NuScenes, that contain highly diverse driving scenarios. Our key contributions are: (1) the development of an optimal solution for object pose and shape estimation over highly varied driving scenarios; (2) a method for robustly calculating object poses and shapes despite potential training and testing discrepancies; and (3) in-depth evaluations of our approach on real-world autonomous vehicle datasets, which showcase its superior performance and generalizability. We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a Cauchy distribution, by considering the location and scale parameters of a sample, and develop a method to calculate the area using the Cauchy distribution's probability density function. This approach will also enable us to determine the confidence limits for the location and scale parameters separately, in the form of a discriminant region for the parameters of interest. While this method will primarily be demonstrated for the location and scale parameters, the proposed approach can be extended to other situations as well. Furthermore, we will present results of numerical investigations of the confidence limits' performance in terms of accuracy and computational speed, along with an examination of their symmetry and independence on the sample size. Additionally, we will provide an example of the application of this method in a real-world analysis. We will also explore an alternative method to tackle this problem, by employing Bayesian inference guided by uniform prior distributions on the location and scale parameters, and driven by the evidence from the data. This method will be based on the probability function of the scaled difference between two random variables following a Cauchy distribution, and will enable us to define a region of Bayesian credibility for the location and scale parameters, by integrating this probability function over different values of the location and scale parameters. We will examine the performance of this credibility method in terms of its accuracy and computational speed, as well as its symmetry and dependence on the sample size. Lastly, we will compare the performance of the confidence disc/square method with the Bayesian credibility method. These methods can be implemented in various statistical software packages, such as Mathematica, MATLAB and Python. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, providing confirmation of lattice QCD predictions. We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions. Furthermore, we find that the kernel of the Dirac operator represents the space of infinitesimal deformations for the canonical connection itself. The structure of this kernel allows us to characterize the moduli space of the canonical connection in terms of its isomorphism to a specific Lie algebra. Lastly, we prove that the moduli space of the canonical connection on a specific non-primitive nearly G2-manifold of four dimensions is isomorphic to a specific Lie algebra. Finally, our research provides a comprehensive illustration of the properties of C-normal weighted composition operators in the $H^2$ space. We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with a new analytical framework, utilizing the radar's unique characteristics to improve network performance. Our techniques, modified slotted ALOHA and CSMA, utilize the radar cross-correlation property to monitor the medium and resist multiple access interference. Our analysis considers the network's properties, such as the radar's modulating function and its significant data transmission duration, and develops efficient user equipment designs, including autoregressive-based radar detectors, to optimize the ALOHA protocol's parameters and minimize collisions in CSMA. Our research extends the ALOHA protocol to support multiple packet transmission and shows that using the radar's cross-correlation property reduces the required number of transmissions, improving the overall network capacity. Our results also demonstrate that using CSMA in FMCW radar networks offers better collision performance and higher network capacity compared to traditional ALOHA. Additionally, our research identifies the optimal CSMA parameters, achieving the maximum network capacity, and our simulations verify the excellent collision performance of the modified medium access techniques in various radar network scenarios. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, biology, medicine, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur's work is representative of a Kantian perspective, while Randall has drawn parallels with modern infinitesimals in the framework of Robinson. This account seeks to reconcile these various interpretations and presents an alternative, three-part account of the calculus as used by Leibniz, drawing on key ideas from modern mathematics: the concept of a Frechet derivative from real analysis, along with topological considerations implicit in Leibniz's use of a convergent infinite sequence in his 'differentials', combined with a singular 'layering' of quantities, analogous to a Cantor set. Recommender Systems, particularly in e-commerce settings, have facilitated a seamless and enjoyable shopping experience for consumers by reducing the overwhelming complexity of available products. To achieve this level of integration, a comprehensive approach is required, incorporating both a user interface and a sophisticated recommendation algorithm. To address the dual objectives of user interface and personalized recommendation, hybrid methods combining various techniques have gained prominence in recent years. A potential hybrid solution integrated context-aware and behavior-based recommender systems is presented in this research, combining the strengths of both paradigms to address the primary challenge of integrating a user interface and a personalized recommendation algorithm. An innovative solution integrates a context-aware component providing a comprehensive product search and a behavior-based component offering a dynamic and adaptive recommendation service. An experimental evaluation of this integrated system was conducted, demonstrating its effectiveness through a combination of theoretical and empirical analysis. The integration of a context-aware and behavior-based recommender system outperformed other hybrid approaches, yielding superior outcomes in terms of coverage and accuracy. Furthermore, a detailed cost-benefit analysis validated the integrated system's robustness and reliability. This characteristic underlies a broader hypothesis regarding the matrix ensembles, which includes specific test cases such as Wigner and GUE matrices. The present investigation extends this hypothesis in two distinct directions: Firstly, it quantifies the rate at which the eigenvalue ratio converges to its limiting value; secondly, it explores the relationship between this hypothesis and a separate theory of 'freeness of type $B$'. Theoretical proofs and statistical analyses underpin these findings, which also suggest new avenues for research in asymptotic freeness and 'freeness of type $B$'. Furthermore, theoretical considerations are supplemented with a range of numerical examples, which highlight the complexity and variability of eigenvalue behavior in unitarily invariant matrix ensembles. Results are also presented for matrices with limited symmetry, as well as for matrices with non-zero trace. The findings also suggest novel connections between the matrix ensembles and general theoretical frameworks. Finally, the relationship between the matrix ensembles and 'freeness of type $B$' is utilized to explain and analyze the behavior of certain probability distributions, such as the ratio of spectral functions of unitarily invariant random matrices. The study offers a comprehensive explanation of the matrix ensembles and their properties, which provide insight into the structure and variability of the eigenvalue ratio in random matrices. The relationship between the matrix ensembles and 'freeness of type $B$' also opens up new avenues for applying this theoretical framework to the analysis of the eigenvalue spectrum. At the same time, the investigation demonstrates that the matrix ensembles can offer insights into the asymptotic behavior of the eigenvalue spectrum. The matrix ensembles can thus be seen as a tool for explaining and analyzing the structure and variability of the eigenvalue ratio in random matrices. The theoretical frameworks, on the other hand, are modified to accommodate the unique characteristics of the random matrices. The study offers a comprehensive explanation of the relationship between the random matrices and the theoretical frameworks. Lastly, the investigation demonstrates that the random matrices can be understood through the lens of 'freeness of type $B$' and asymptotic freeness. The matrix ensembles can thus be seen as a natural manifestation of these theoretical frameworks. The connection between the random matrices and the theoretical frameworks is a fundamental one, and it is continuously refined and extended throughout the investigation.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered. For each of these themes, we provide a uniform set of theoretical contributions and a practical online monitoring algorithm. Experimental evidence demonstrates that these algorithms perform well even under more complex conditions. As a fundamental aspect, our work considers the special case of infeasible specifications and how timing discrepancies affect monitoring accuracy. This is supplemented by a theoretical analysis of monitoring algorithm complexity. Finally, we examine the relationship between the generative power of specifying languages and the capability to monitor them. This involves establishing bounds on when this capability exists and exploring its implications for the entire realm of real-time specifications. This paper subsumes the authors' prior work on online monitoring of real-time systems, offering a comprehensive study of monitoring in the precise model and using the same zone-based framework. This includes general-purpose monitoring algorithms for the core problems, along with additional algorithmic insights and a complexity examination. This paper further extends its consideration to the special cases of infeasible specifications and the effects of timing discrepancies, along with establishing bounds on when monitoring is feasible and exploring these implications for the entire realm of real-time specifications. This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on reducing the computational cost by taking advantage of small coefficients that arise during the solving process. Our study utilizes the ALC (Algebraic Linear Codes) method, where we evaluate polynomials at specific points that are the minimal roots of a special degree-$N$ polynomial, $N$ being the number of variables in the system. By analyzing the minimum values of coefficients in the evaluated polynomials, we establish new bounds for the probability of error occurrence, similar to the Guruswami-Stern's bounds, and refine them to accommodate various error patterns. Furthermore, we leverage these bounds to develop a new early termination technique, allowing us to stop the solving process if the estimated error probability exceeds a predetermined threshold, without compromising the correctness of the output, thus saving computational cost. Our technique achieves a notable $16\%$ reduction in computational cost compared to existing methods, while also exhibiting higher solvability rates and a $4\%$ reduction in the required degree of the error-correcting code for a given error probability. These improvements significantly outperform the state-of-the-art ALC methods, making the approach more efficient and practical. Our research also includes numerical examples and experimental evidence supporting these claims, and demonstrating the behavior of error probability under varying conditions, which is known as the 'accuracy-decision boundary', and shows that our early termination technique can correctly identify whether to stop or continue solving a polynomial system, matching the 'lazy evaluation' approach in the symbolic annealing method. These findings are further validated by the extensive numerical evaluations presented in the paper. Finally, we also develop a new approach to dynamically determine the optimal degree of the polynomial used to estimate the error probability, outperforming existing methods and showcasing improved results in both the average and worst-case scenarios. These contributions significantly advance the state-of-the-art in solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors, with faster and more efficient computation, improved probability estimates, and refined bounds that generalize well to the worst-case scenario. Additionally, we have freely made available the source code used in this research, allowing other researchers to reproduce our results and study the behavior of error probability under different conditions. This code is publicly accessible at the specified URL. In summary, our research has delivered a breakthrough in solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors, outperforming existing methods in computational efficiency while providing improved generalizations of existing results. By introducing a qubit with arbitrary occupation, we find that the system remains in an entangled dark state until a transition to a bright state occurs, releasing a photon bundle. The emission pattern exhibits features of $n$-photon bundles, with a peak-emission rate significantly higher than that of single photons, and demonstrating a larger photon indistinguishability. The emergence of super-Rabi oscillations and the system's ability to remain in a dark state enable the conservation of angular momentum in the cavity, resulting in the parity-symmetry-protected emission of photon bundles. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse graph's node count under the scenario where at most $p$ out of $n$ nodes can maliciously provide incorrect data to other nodes, akin to a $(p)$-fault model. Our focus is single-blockchain VDFs as our model for synchronized computations. We establish an estimated value for a network's size, proving it to be within an additive and multiplicative error factor of the actual value. Our work particularly considers the case where the malicious nodes can intentionally deceive others by offering inaccurate metric values, such as degree or local diameter, while also exploring the scenario where only a specific metric value can be trusted. We achieve this task with the help of a novel distance estimation approach and construct an all-embracing protocol by integrating various sub-protocols designed to estimate a network's diameter, degree distribution characteristics, and node interconnectivity. Ultimately, our protocol achieves an estimated node count with an additive and multiplicative error factor of approximately $\pm p$ with an estimated running time of $\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{n^3\lambda^2}{\pi^2p^2}\text{ VDF runtime}\right)$. Here, the runtime of a single VDF computation is denoted as $\lambda$. We believe our findings to be valuable contributions to the field of distributed computing, particularly in the area of estimating a network's node count under the presence of malicious nodes. We firmly believe that our proposed solution enjoys robustness due to its resilience in the presence of malicious nodes and the consideration of estimated metric values. Furthermore, it exhibits efficiency as it can function without the need for a central node or a specific node, and even in the worst case, it achieves an estimated node count with an additive error factor of approximately $O(p)$. Finally, it boasts a low communication complexity of $O(\log^2 n + \log \frac{n^2}{p^2} + \log \frac{n}{p})$. Lastly, it boasts terminal complexity that is directly proportional to the communication bandwidth, that is $O(\max \left\{ \log \frac{n}{p}, \log \frac{n}{p}\right\})$. In practical scenarios, the forecasting of time series data is frequently characterized by the presence of multiple dimensional time series components that are interconnected. To address this challenge, an innovative framework called AGCNet is introduced, which dynamically constructs relationships across different dimensions of multiple time series. The core component of this network is the adaptive graph convolutional module, where the graph's matrix is adaptively modified to highlight significant correlations between different dimensions of a time series. By applying this module in a neural network structure, the forecasting of multiple time series with varying lengths of horizons becomes possible. The effectiveness of this adaptive framework is demonstrated through its applications on synthetic and real-world data, specifically in the prediction of PM values from multi-dimensional sensor data. Furthermore, the framework's adaptability and accuracy are compared with those of traditional methods, including a classical physics-based model and more advanced machine learning algorithms. The results consistently show that the adaptive framework yields the most accurate predictions across all evaluation metrics. Consequently, the framework presents a valuable solution for the practical forecasting of multidimensional time series data that is frequently encountered in industrial applications. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers to enhance student performance; and 2) preserving labeled information to maintain ranking accuracy after distillation. We introduce a new distillation method, PILE, which utilizes a logistic function to model a single teacher's ranking capability and incorporates iteration-based correction to refine predictions. Additionally, PILE incorporates labeled information into the distillation process through pair-wise comparison. Experimental results demonstrate that PILE outperforms current methods by effectively utilizing multiple teachers and labeled data to achieve higher accuracy and faster training convergence. PILE has been successfully applied in a commercial search platform, demonstrating robust performance in real-world scenarios. The code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/mayuweipk/PILE.

It's a critical component in various fluid dynamics models, particularly when coupled with heat and scalar transport equations. As a broad class of problems, scalar and vector transport equations are investigated using semi-implicit discretisations with Raviart-Thomas finite elements. However, this approach's accuracy is limited, leading to a lower-order approximation when using the lowest-order Raviart-Thomas elements. To improve the semi-implicit discretisation with the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements, we introduce and study two post-processing schemes. These schemes enhance the accuracy of the approximated scalar and vector field values at certain points, compared to their corresponding cell values. Numerical experiments are conducted to evaluate the introduced post-processing methods, achieving a fourfold increase in accuracy compared to the standard semi-implicit Raviart-Thomas discretisation. Furthermore, we successfully implemented these post-processing methods in complex 3D simulations, achieving a fourfold increase in accuracy compared to the standard semi-implicit Raviart-Thomas discretisation. In a comparison with an explicit finite element method, we observed that the post-processing methods reduced the oscillations and errors associated with that approach, while also minimizing the additional computational cost. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified framework that seamlessly integrates these methodologies. Fairness constraints can be imposed on specific layers, and a novel regularization term ensures compliance with differential privacy standards. Furthermore, our approach scales efficiently to process large datasets, as evidenced by the evaluation on multiple UCI datasets and the CIFAR-10 benchmark. Federated learning, in conjunction with our method, achieves an impressive accuracy of 85.1% on the CIFAR-10 dataset, surpassing existing state-of-the-art solutions by 2%. Moreover, this approach offers substantial improvements in computational efficiency and statistical privacy compared to current methods. Comprehensive experimentation, including ablation studies on real-world image data (e.g., ImageNet), confirms the superiority of our approach in balancing predictive performance with privacy and fairness considerations. A video demonstration and the source code are available for review at https://github.com/pmehta/federated_egan. This work has potential applications in various domains, including self-driving cars and medical diagnosis, where fairness and privacy are often of paramount importance. Ultimately, our approach provides a resilient and adaptable framework for training robust, fair, and private models in distributed settings. A brief tutorial on the underlying techniques is available at https://pmehta.github.io/federated_egan/. Increased dissipation enhances Wada basin stability, measured by the number of Wada sites within the basin. A notable outcome is that weak dissipation actually prolongs the lifespan of Wada basins. We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, inflows, and outflows being represented by measures on Borel spaces. This investigation arises from a lack of optimal solutions for the production model, which poses a nonlinear first-order conservation law with respect to time and a nonlinear transport equation with respect to space. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of a weak measure-valued solution as a solution that can be approximated by a sequence of solutions to related finite-dimensional optimization problems. This approach is analogous to the original model, but with the added constraint of a perfect fluid, and offers a viable solution strategy, particularly suited for problems involving many production lines and warehouses. Furthermore, we outline a theoretical framework that could lead to a candidate solution for the original optimization problem. A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Some methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, while others construct features rich in information about OoD examples, enabling improved handling but often at the cost of compromised in-distribution performance. We introduce an approach for constructing detailed OoD features in a way that allows for simpler optimization, resulting in better generalization. These features, derived from autoencoders trained to locate the density boundary between in-distribution and OoD data, are used to model the classifier's bias towards these features. We then apply a straightforward regularization scheme to break this bias, achieving high performance both in-distribution and on OoD tasks. The proposed method surpasses several prominent baselines in an empirical evaluation of its ability to handle OoD examples. Furthermore, the generated features offer valuable insights into what features lead to predictive uncertainties and highlight the method's limitations on data with unforeseen backgrounds. Furthermore, in practical settings, informed treatment rules are often chosen based on underlying structures, such as those in Han et al. (2019) and Zhao et al. (2020). Nonetheless, we acknowledge that overfitting can be a critical concern in some cases and encourage continued exploration of the design of informed model-agnostic learning methods.

Our rejoiners also address the remaining comments from discussants, but space constraints limit further discussion here. We're grateful to the discussants, editors, and reviewers for their input and feedback, which significantly enhanced the final version of our paper.

In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively synthesize dependent effects, however these may produce inflated Type 1 errors in cases of a limited number of studies.  In order to address this issue, we will present novel cluster-robust estimators that incorporate an empirical Bayes method for estimating between-study variance, these estimators yield accurate results even in scenarios with a low number of studies.  Similar estimators will also be developed for the second key quantity in meta-regression, effect size gradient.  The proposed estimators will be demonstrated on realistic data and compared with established methods through simulations, ultimately showcasing their benefits and limitations. In addition to standard applications, these new estimators will facilitate the modeling of publication bias based on study quality.  The proposed estimators will be further validated through Bayesian evidence and comparative analysis. The proposed methods will be exemplified on real data from 14 studies examining the relationship between cannabis use and schizophrenia. The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different values of a key coefficient that influence broadening calculations. Results obtained via numerical analysis in the color dipole approach are compared with corresponding findings from perturbative QCD. Nuclear transverse momentum imbalances at the LHC energy are examined for both rapidity and longitudinal and transverse momentum dependencies. Our calculations demonstrate that model predictions can diverge significantly, especially for transverse momentum imbalances at various angles and high rapidity. However, predictions from the different models become more aligned as the rapidity increases, reflecting collective behavior. Furthermore, broadening effects are found to dominate transverse momentum imbalances observed in high-energy proton-proton collisions. At the LHC energy, nuclear broadening significantly impacts transverse momentum imbalances, and variations across different models can substantially affect this phenomenon. We conducted an in-depth examination of the statistical properties of a three-body system, specifically those consisting of one massive object and two objects of different masses orbiting around it, as predicted by Lehmann et al.'s (2020) flux-based three-body model. This analytical model was compared to the corresponding numerical n-body model, with a particular focus on the distribution of the three bodies' relative fluxes. Our analysis revealed that this model accurately reproduces the long-term behavior of the three-body system, specifically the stationary long-term distribution of the binding energies and the distribution of the orbital eccentricities. However, the flux-based model fails to capture the equal mass distribution accurately. Our results also indicate that the binary-uniform phase space approximation is the primary contributor to the long-term distribution of the binding energies, whereas the binary-binary and equal mass phases contribute equally to the flux-based model's inaccuracies. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrated that the long-term distribution of the binding energies is insensitive to the initial conditions of the three-body system. Ultimately, our findings validate the flux-based statistical prediction of the three-body system's long-term behavior. Our analysis methods are versatile and can be applied to other statistical predictions for n-body systems with n ≥ 3. This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations to the category of complete metric spaces with continuous functions as morphisms.

Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents modified constraints where it is proven that $a_n > 2^{\frac{n}{4} + \frac{1}{4} \ln n - \frac{1}{2} \ln \ln n}$. Additionally, the problem is refined to restrict a linear combination of elements from the set, with the result showing $a_n > 2^{\frac{n}{3} + \frac{2}{3} \ln n - \frac{2}{3} \ln \ln n}$. Another variation of the problem involves combining numbers from the set in base $b \geq 2$ and imposes a digit limit of $\lambda b$. The result shows $a_n > b^{\frac{n}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \ln n - \frac{1}{2} \ln \ln n}$. All of these results break the current record of $a_n > c \cdot b^{\frac{n}{2}}/\sqrt{n}$. Another problem is proposed and solved under the assumption that the elements in the set form an arithmetic sequence. Also discussed is a version of the problem where only nonnegative integers are used. In this version, it is proven that $a_n < 2^{n/2 + 1/2 \ln n + 3/2 \ln \ln n}$. Another problem related to this version is proposed. Lastly, it is confirmed that the lower bound $a_n > 2^{n/3 - 2/3 \ln n + 2/3 \ln \ln n}$ holds under the assumption that all elements in the set are integers. All of these results update the current record of $a_n > c \cdot 2^{n/3 - 2/3 \ln n + 2/3 \ln \ln n}$. Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers by rolling along them, as shown in recent studies. This phenomenon was previously proposed to be the result of a physical force known as gecko force, which causes the virus to adhere to neighboring molecules and move in tandem with them. However, the underlying physics driving this motion remains unclear. Our computer-based simulation model re-created the virus's geometric structure and tested different physical forces contributing to this motion. We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have bluer V-R colors and higher star formation rates (H$\alpha$ equivalent widths) compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher H$\alpha$ equivalent widths and bluer V-R colors. We linked U-type warps to tidal forces and star formation, proposing a new model: U galaxies may be akin to 'jellyfish' galaxies, formed by the interplay of tidal forces and starburst activity. This theory is supported by the fact that U galaxies are more common in groups/clusters and U galaxies without neighbors primarily exhibit high star formation rates. S-type warps, on the other hand, are equally associated with tidal forces and intrinsic processes. Our findings are consistent with the idea that group/cluster tides can induce U-type warps and trigger star bursts in galaxies. Furthermore, U galaxies may serve as an early warning sign for the transformation of disk galaxies into jellyfish galaxies and potentially Tidal Dwarf Galaxies. Our research is the initial phase of a comprehensive study on warped galaxies, and future work will focus on U galaxies in isolated environments and their long-term evolution. For this initial research, data were obtained from SDSS DR7. Our analyses included 8192 massive, edge-on disk galaxies, and we plan to extend this study to a larger dataset from the MaNGA survey, encompassing both blue and red galaxies. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.
