The global pandemic of misinformation dissemination has been exacerbated by social media platforms, leading to severe consequences such as the spread of COVID-19 misinformation in India, which resulted in a government-imposed ban on WhatsApp for two months. In an effort to combat misinformation, WhatsApp introduced a feature limiting the number of times a single message can be forwarded to others. This study investigates the impact of this limitation in a large-scale experiment conducted among WhatsApp users in India. Our analysis reveals that the limitation reduced the dissemination of misinformation to others, but led the initial sender to forward the information to more people, particularly in rural areas. Furthermore, the limitation caused misinformation disseminators to exhibit more persistent behavior, particularly when the initial message was forwarded from another country. Interestingly, the limitation did not reduce the spread of politics-related information, but rather led to an increase in the number of forward events involved. While the limitation showed promise in curtailing misinformation dissemination, its effectiveness was largely undermined by the actions of the initial senders. To inform the design of more robust interventions, our study provides a detailed analysis of the complex nuances underpinning the spread of misinformation. Our findings align with the self-reinforcement theory, which posits that the initial sender's stakes in the conversation elevate their commitment to disseminating the information. Additionally, our study shows that the spread of misinformation can be predicted by key characteristics of the sender, the recipient, and the information itself, similar to existing research on social media platforms. In an effort to combat misinformation, our study proposes an alternative approach that targets the initial senders, the key contributors to the spread of misinformation. We also acknowledge the limitations of our study and suggest potential avenues for further research. The data collected from our experiment total 11.97 million messages, amounting to 1.52 terabytes, and are available on a data sharing platform for the benefit of the research community. Our study provides a framework that can be adapted and used by researchers to study misinformation on other social media platforms, as well as to evaluate the effectiveness of novel countermeasures. In recognition of the pressing need to address the misinformation epidemic, our study demonstrates a novel approach to combating misinformation by limiting message forwarding, an easily understandable and relatable concept. We investigated a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from each other. It's assumed that individuals experience mutations at a specified rate under an infinitely many alleles model, resulting in random genetic variations that evolve independently over time. Conditioned on the population size becoming infinitely large, the frequency spectrum of these genetic variations converges almost surely to a continuous function. The frequency spectrum represents the average number of genetic variations within a specific allele frequency range. Two specific models were explored in more detail: a model with regularly occurring births and a model where each individual has a fixed number of children. In both cases, we derived precise expressions for the frequency spectrum, and through comparison with simulations, we validated these expressions as highly accurate approximations for a range of parameter values. Furthermore, we discovered that the frequency spectrum exhibits a symmetrical pattern, and the central portion dominates the frequency spectrum with a specific asymptotic contribution, indicating that the frequency spectrum is primarily determined by the central portion. Additionally, we derived explicit formulas for the average number of genetic variations within a specific allele frequency range in the frequency spectrum. These formulas demonstrate the relationship between genetic variation and allele frequency, and the frequency spectrum's curvature is directly proportional to this relationship. With these insights, we were able to effectively tackle the problem of estimating the population's effective population size based on the frequency spectrum, and we proposed a method of frequency-spectrum-based estimation that is easy to use and does not require knowledge of the distribution of genetic variations. The method was validated through comparison with simulations, and it emerges that the proposed estimator is highly accurate and robust across a wide range of parameter values. Specifically, we found that the proposed estimator is particularly effective and robust when the population experiences a rapid growth in size. Furthermore, we explored the feasibility and usefulness of the proposed estimator in a real-world application by estimating the effective population size of the genus Rattus based on the frequency spectrum of mitochondrial DNA variations from ancient DNA samples spanning the last 200,000 years. The results show that the proposed estimator is capable of capturing the changes in the effective population size caused by population dynamics and these changes correlate well with the expected changes in the effective population size based on a widely accepted model of population size changes in the genus Rattus. The results also reveal that the effective population size remained relatively constant at around 10,000 individuals for the majority of the genus Rattus's evolution, and it only increased rapidly

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. By selectively amplifying key input characteristics and suppressing irrelevant ones, AReLU enables our system to prioritize artifact-related features. Our proposed system was applied to the logical access task using the ASVSpoof2019 dataset and demonstrated improved performance compared to systems utilizing standard, non-adaptive activation functions. Specifically, our AReLU-based system exhibited a 21.91% equal error rate (EER) reduction and outperformed state-of-the-art countermeasures in various evaluations. Furthermore, our experimental findings highlighted the adaptive nature of AReLU and its feature-dependent weight calculations, which facilitated enhanced discrimination of artificial speech characteristics. With its ability to dynamically filter input features, our AReLU-based spoofing countermeasure system serves as a versatile framework for speech authentication tasks. First, a full supergravity model with a heavy spatio-temporal gradient is constructed and the Goldstino degree of freedom is isolated. Subsequently, the supergravity model is simplified into an effective field theory, the coefficients of which are determined by the supergravity model's properties. Effective field theories have previously been used successfully to describe dark matter and the Higgs boson. The goal of this research is to create an effective field theory of inflation that is consistent with the fundamental theory of supergravity. An example of such an effective field theory is developed using a Wess-Zumino model in three dimensions. The resulting effective field theory possesses an $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetry and features a single scalar field along with three fermionic fields, the coefficients of whose interactions depend on the three-dimensional Planck mass. A crucial process in network security involves identifying protocols dynamically, a concept that has become increasingly essential for sophisticated threat identification.  Both commercial and open-source monitoring tools, such as Bro and Suricata, rely on this capability to detect potential threats.  Although a significant amount of research focuses on evaluating static protocol detection accuracy, very little attention has been given to verifying the reliability of dynamic protocol detection.  In this research, we assess the open-source network security monitoring tool, NSE, examining the reliability of its dynamic protocol detection features through thorough testing.  Our study reveals significant inaccuracies in some of NSE's detection methods: some falsely detect protocol usage in specific ports, while others fail to correctly identify the protocol used by certain applications.  These flaws can potentially lead to spurious alarms generated by misleading traffic analysis.  To highlight the vulnerabilities, we describe multiple tactics that attackers can employ to deceive network security monitors employing inaccurate or flawed dynamic protocol detection.  These tactics encompass both targeted and stealthy attacks, as well as scenarios involving malicious actors operating remotely.  Our research further discusses potential causes of these inaccuracies, including the reliance of some detection methods on ambiguous or incomplete traffic patterns.  To improve the reliability of dynamic protocol detection, we suggest possible enhancements, such as incorporating deep packet inspection, utilizing more robust traffic pattern identification, and integrating with firewalls for supplementary verification.  Ultimately, our research emphasizes the need for regular and systematic testing of dynamic protocol detection mechanisms to ensure precision and robustness in open-source network security monitoring tools.  By doing so, we can enhance the accuracy of threat detection and ultimately contribute to more effective security incident detection.  In addition to presenting these research findings, we have also created a publicly accessible testing framework that allows for the evaluation of dynamic protocol detection capabilities in network security monitoring tools.  This resource can be utilized by security researchers and developers to assess and improve the accuracy of dynamic protocol detection in both existing and future security monitoring tools.  A comprehensive dataset is included with the paper that demonstrates various dynamic protocol detection scenarios, providing context for the research findings presented.  The dataset can be accessed through the following link: https://tinyurl.com/NSE-DPD-Data.  The public nse-tool repository, where the network security monitor code is stored, can be accessed through the following link: https://github.com/secure-gateway/nse.  The public repository of our testing framework, named DPD-TF, can be accessed through the following link: https://github.com/secure-gateway/DP

Initially, we apply our approach to measure a complete three-photon GHZ state across three dimensions and then extend it to multi-photon systems within higher dimensional settings. In our model, both quantum projection measurement and parasitic function measurements are employed to achieve thorough analysis. In experiments involving high-dimensional systems, quantum projection measurement can be impractical due to alignment issues, making our approach applicable to real-world experiments. Intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRSs) are gaining attention due to their ability to optimize wireless communication systems without the limitations of linear processing. However, the performance of these systems is heavily dependent on accurate channel estimation, a complex task due to the numerous parameters involved in IRSs. Current estimation methods often rely on pilot symbols sent by individual users, which can lead to underutilized bandwidth and lower system efficiency. In this study, a novel cascaded channel estimation technique is proposed for multiuser massive MIMO systems aided by an IRS. By treating the IRS as a cascaded channel, a comprehensive channel matrix is estimated using pilot symbols, after which user-specific channel vectors are derived through optimization. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed technique outperforms traditional pilot-based methods in terms of scaling with the number of users and reflection symbols. Additionally, the proposed technique yields better performance in terms of pilot bandwidth efficiency and user data rate. Furthermore, the proposed technique is shown to be compatible with popular optimization methods for maximizing sum rate and minimizing energy consumption. Simulation results confirm that the proposed technique outperforms these benchmark optimization methods in various scenarios. In particular, when the IRS is closely located to the users, the proposed technique is found to effectively mitigate channel scaling and improve performance without detailed channel knowledge. Furthermore, the proposed technique is found to be resilient to IRS element quantization and remains accurate even at high levels of phase quantization. Simulation results show that the proposed technique achieves nearly optimal performance even when the IRS elements are quantized to a limited number of phases. In particular, when two phases are used for each IRS element, the proposed technique is found to lose only 0.05% of its maximum possible performance value. In contrast, the performance loss associated with pilot-based methods increases exponentially with the number of quantized phases. Specifically, when two phases are used for each IRS element, the performance loss of pilot-based methods amounts to 2.35%, 14.3%, and 30.8% of their maximum possible performance value for 4, 16, and 64 quantized phases, respectively. Consequently, the proposed technique is found to be a highly efficient solution for estimating the cascaded channel of multiuser massive MIMO systems aided by an IRS. In particular, when compared to pilot-based methods, the proposed technique is found to achieve higher user data rates, reduce the required pilot bandwidth, increase the efficiency of pilot bandwidth utilization, decrease the required power for a given target data rate, and decrease the required number of symbols for a given target sum rate

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a unique dataset with over 740,000 articles from over 300 local news outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, local news COVID coverage varied based on the severity of infections in the covered areas, with certain demographic groups receiving more COVID-related news depending on the local news outlet they relied on. Furthermore, local news outlets that primarily served older audiences covered COVID more frequently than those serving younger demographics. Our research provides critical insights for journalists, managers, and researchers involved in aggregating and disseminating COVID-related news to various audiences. It also highlights the significance of supporting and sustaining the role of local news in informing and educating communities, particularly during times of crisis. Given the ongoing coverage of COVID and other global health issues, such as SARS-CoV-2 variants and flu seasons, the findings of this research will remain relevant and valuable in the future. Ultimately, this project demonstrates the potential of online monitoring systems in studying news topics that cannot be captured through Google Trends or other popular aggregators. While these methods can provide comprehensive coverage of widespread topics, they may fail to detect the unique perspectives and stories provided by local news outlets, which are essential in understanding the diverse experiences of communities affected by COVID. It is stressed that local news coverage brought unique perspectives to the public discourse during the pandemic, showcasing their significance in informing audiences. Therefore, local news deserves continued support, especially through initiatives like news aggregation and sharing on social media platforms, to ensure equity in community access to accurate and diverse COVID-related information. To enhance fairness in local news coverage, it is recommended that news aggregators and disseminators prioritize and mirror a range of topics from the local news outlets their audiences rely on. This can help counterbalance the undercoverage of COVID and other critical regional issues, ultimately promoting more equitable and informed communities. To meet this need, our research proposes the development of a comprehensive and open-access news aggregator system that reflects the diverse perspectives of local news outlets accurately and disseminates a range of topics effectively. Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters help engineers prevent time-consuming operations and save valuable resources by predicting membership using hash functions. Although efficient, Bloom filters can produce false positives, which can be reduced using more compact alternatives like Bloom-like filters and Bloom filters with non-uniform distributions. These improvements, however, come at a higher computational cost. In contrast, xor filters, originally introduced by Tarann et al. in 2013, offer equal or better performance improvements compared to these earlier solutions. We build upon their work by integrating Bloom filters' functionality into a general filter class, which we use to evaluate and optimize existing solutions, including xor filters. Through efficient implementations of these filters, we demonstrate the superiority of xor filters in both memory usage and processing speed. Furthermore, we introduce a new algorithm, insert-and-replace, which integrates elements of Bloom filters and xor filters to achieve optimal performance in both memory consumption and processing efficiency. This method surpasses existing solutions in all evaluation criteria. The implementation of these filters is freely available as the xorf library for Python. It includes a range of filter types that can be used as drop-in replacements for standard Bloom filters. The source code can be found at https://github.com/constme/xorf. The xorf library supports both Python 3 and 4, as well as native compilation on Windows, macOS, and Linux systems. It is fully self-contained and does not rely on other third-party libraries for its operation. In particular, we integrated the insert-and-replace algorithm into the hashlib library for Python to provide a straightforward and easy-to-use solution for replacing existing Bloom filters. This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data, then create a consensus gradient from these clusters. Furthermore, it showcases robustness in diverse parameter scenarios and maintains comparable performance to the baseline federated learning method. Ultimately, our method demonstrates exemplary ecological, efficiency, and security properties. A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic. Furthermore, we provide a new simplification of the Borel Wadge collapse over totally Borel second-countable spaces and offer additional applications and simplifications to prior results. Additionally, we show that any non-trivial Borel Wadge class contains an element that can be identified using a $\Sigma^1_2$-uniform schema. This, in turn, allows us to derive an independence result within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Sigma^1_2$-I system of second-order arithmetic. Finally, we offer an effective classification of subsets of standard Baire space relative to any countable ordinal $\alpha$, showing that almost all subsets of this space belong to a specific Borel Wadge class determined by $\alpha$. This result allows us to derive a collection of related findings and applications. Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are increasingly being used for object detection tasks, however, they pose significant computational challenges during training. Pruning, a method to reduce the network's size and computational load, can be utilized but has generally been applied to specific layers separately, disregarding the overall effect on the network. ClickTrain efficiently addresses this issue by integrating a unified pruning strategy throughout the entire network structure. At each iteration, a weight pruning matrix is determined and used to directly remove unnecessary weights from the weights matrix, thereby eliminating accuracy loss and bypassing gradient backpropagation. This approach avoids the computational bottleneck often associated with training pruned neural networks and allows for the precise control of the pruned matrix, thereby achieving the optimal trade-off between computational efficiency and accuracy. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the versatility and efficiency of ClickTrain and highlight its ability to accurately represent the effects of pruned matrices on specific layers, further solidifying its potential as a pioneering end-to-end pruning framework. This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from noncommutative lattices by incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$. A new semantics model is introduced, specifically tailored for substructural modal logics. By applying duality principles, we demonstrate that every modal logic derived from the full Lambek calculus has a Kripke model, if it adheres to a specific structural rule. Furthermore, we establish a dual relationship between certain mathematical structures, specifically modal algebras and topological Kripke spaces, utilizing a topological model developed from Priestley spaces. As a result, we prove that every modal logic derived from the full Lambek calculus with modal operators is sound in its corresponding algebra and has a corresponding topological Kripke space. Moreover, we identify a critical limitation on the structural rule framework, stemming from a fundamental property of topological Kripke spaces, which leads to a weakening of the underlying structural rule. This finding is substantiated by an example involving a modal logic derived from the full Lambek calculus with modal operators. Additionally, we present an algorithm for transforming a modal formula into its equivalent canonical form within the context of our developed topological model. This is made possible by a method for eliminating the modal operators $\Box$ and $\Diamond$ from a modal formula, if it does not contain any negations. This method essentially converts the modal formula into its corresponding canonical form. Consequently, we demonstrate that every modal logic derived from the full Lambek calculus with modal operators has a corresponding canonical algebra. This research is an extension of our previous work on substructural modal logics. This material is based on a doctoral dissertation, which was defended on December 20, 2011, at the University of Insubria, Italy. A preliminary version of this research was published in the 2011 IEEE Symposium on Logic in Computer Science. This research is also a subset of my recent research, which will be presented at the 2012 IEEE Conference on Logic and Religion. In particular, a more detailed discussion of the underlying mathematical structures can be found in my recent research. This material is also a subset of a forthcoming book on substructural modal logics, which is currently under review. Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) are used to optimize systems with performance and constraint limitations. Current algorithms for finding optimal CMDP policies often employ interior-point methods, which assume a prior knowledge of the epsilon-epsilon optimal policy. In contrast, our approach uses a primal-dual algorithm to directly find an epsilon-optimal policy without specifying the epsilon value in advance. Our method integrates three components: an value function approximation, a policy relaxation, and a dual variable adjustment. Through iterative calculation, it is mathematically proven that our algorithm reaches an epsilon-optimal policy in a specified number of iterations. The algorithm's applicability is demonstrated in two real-world scenarios: a parking cost model and a parking duration management problem. The former is optimized using a linear programming approach, while the latter employs a more complex Julia julia programming model, which requires integer variables to account for the limited parking duration. Both scenarios successfully use our proposed algorithm to find suitable policies. Furthermore, it is shown that our algorithm significantly outperforms current interior-point methods by reducing computation time. In particular, it is found that our algorithm takes 1-3 orders of magnitude less computation time to achieve similar results compared to interior-point methods. Therefore, it is recommended to use our proposed algorithm, which offers a more efficient solution to optimizing CMDPs. Properties of the manifold are then reflected in spectral properties of the superconformal quantum mechanics Hamiltonian. We demonstrate that eigenvalues, by influencing a sheaf cohomology, enable us to calculate volume forms on the manifold's fiber product of Lagrangian submanifolds. Ultimately, an intriguing connection emerges between eigenvalue distribution and sheaf cohomology across various weights, ultimately resulting in the computation of holomorphic Euler characteristics for the quiver's tensor product of vector bundles. Our methods provide an alternative to utilizing discrete invariant theories in computing this characteristic. Additionally, we explore an extension of our approach to superconformal field theory, though the reasoning behind the cohomology vanishing in quantum mechanics does not directly apply to the field theory case. Instead, we rely on the properties of holomorphic volume forms and volumes of manifolds with a special type of symmetry. We examine the relationship between network architecture and disease propagation in the contact process using numerical methods. Our analysis reveals that highly clustered networks with small average degree tend to have a higher critical infection rate than their small-world counterparts. Furthermore, a higher fraction of the network's nodes connected to the initial disease source results in a higher critical infection rate. This increased connectivity exacerbates disease spread, leading to a higher critical infection rate. To understand these findings, we developed an analytical model for disease propagation in complex networks, which we were able to solve exactly. Our numerical and analytical results align, demonstrating how network topology influences disease spread in these systems. Our work may contribute to a broader understanding of contagion dynamics in network models and potentially shed light on real-world pandemics. Our source code is available at https://github.com/pauluszkowalski/contact-process-in-complex-networks for reproducibility purposes. Additionally, we generated a figure showing the relationship between network clustering and disease propagation speed (see supplementary information). Actor-critic reinforcement learning is commonly employed in robotics due to its versatility in a range of control tasks. However, its practical implementation often results in suboptimal policy outcomes owing to the limitations inherent in the actor-critic model. To overcome these shortcomings, our approach integrates the actor-critic model with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) for a hybrid framework termed the Hamiltonian Policy. In doing so, our novel method leverages the advantages of HMC, specifically the Hamiltonian dynamics, to enhance the policy. Consequently, the new framework facilitates more precise exploration within the state space and enhances sampling efficiency. Furthermore, our approach permits the utilization of highly efficient gradient estimators, thereby enabling the training of complex policies. Through comprehensive evaluations on diverse control tasks, our results demonstrate that the Hamiltonian Policy exhibits superior performance to established baseline models. Moreover, our findings show that the integration of HMC leads to a boost in data efficiency during the training process. To substantiate the efficacy of our approach, we provide in-depth visualizations and present an intuitive case study to illustrate the benefits of Hamiltonian Policy over traditional actor-critic models. Furthermore, our experiments involve a comparison with state-of-the-art continuous control methods, specifically TD3 and SAC, which reveal a notable enhancement in performance. Specifically, our results show that Hamiltonian Policy achieves a notable increase of up to 30% in the success rate in the hard version of the latent ridge environment, and a notable increase of up to 57% in the cumulative rewards in the pendulum swing-up environment, with similar computational requirements. We will refer to the number $k$ that produces a given prime $p$ as the $\textbf{generator}$ of that prime. Pairs of twin primes have the unique characteristic of sharing a $\textbf{common generator}$. As a result, searching for these twin primes at the level of their respective generators makes practical sense. In fact, by utilizing this new strategy, we are able to prove that the $\textbf{Hyperbolic Twin Prime Conjecture}$ also holds true. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing environments poses a significant challenge for advanced robotic systems. In order to effectively move through space, a robot must be able to adjust its movement to fit the shape of obstacles in its path, thereby altering its planned route accordingly. This study presents an innovative layered control system for a robot that enables real-time autonomous movement around various obstacles through a combination of decision-making strategies utilizing sensor data. A high-level decision-making module incorporates information from sonar sensors to identify the main path of the robot's movement, while a lower-level control system utilizes a simulation environment to optimize the robot's trajectory around specific obstacles. Both layers operate in real-time, allowing for seamless and efficient movement. The system's performance was tested and validated through a series of experiments using an autonomous mobile robot equipped with sonar sensors and a PC-based control system. The results demonstrate a strong correlation between the robot's navigation commands and the data from sonar sensors, confirming the system's ability to provide a safe and efficient path for the robot's movement. The system has been successfully tested in various environments with different types of obstacles, as shown in the accompanying video available at the link. A new approach called Bayesian pessimism is proposed for creating optimal policy models in offline settings. Traditional pessimism methods in offline reinforcement learning often concentrate on minimizing the worst-case value function. However, this universal minimization can result in over-cautious policies. To address this issue, we developed a quantitative framework to guide the construction of pessimism models. Our Bayesian pessimism method uses a posterior expectation of the worst-case value function, striking a balance between extreme caution and riskiness. A straightforward algorithm is introduced to approximate the Bayesian pessimism model, and its theoretical validity and practical effectiveness are established through proven guarantees and successful applications in practical scenarios. Moreover, our method exhibits improved performance over state-of-the-art methods in simulated experiments. The code for our approach can be found at https://github.com/naoto120/bayesian_pessimism. A detailed theoretical analysis is provided in the supplement at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.04126. Our method has been successfully applied in a real-world online learning application, as described in the supplement. In particular, a practical case involves using Bayesian pessimism to predict the likely outcome of a recommended action in a therapy regime for treating depression with antidepressant medication. These types of data are commonly found in ecological studies, where the presence of a species in a sample is often binary. Researchers often apply hierarchical clustering to analyze such data, using distance metrics like the Bray-Curtis, binary Euclidean, or City-block metrics. This study examines the effectiveness of these traditional methods in retaining the underlying structure of the data, as well as alternative clustering approaches like K-means and SCALES, which are designed for binary data. A comprehensive evaluation strategy is employed to compare the methods, using summary statistics like the Bray-Curtis index, a metric developed for evaluating community similarity. Results from simulations and an actual ecological data set reveal that SCALES performs exceptionally well in retaining the underlying structure of the data, even when the data is subject to error. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the best clustering approach depends on the data and evaluates different clustering approaches using multiple criteria. These findings are consistent across different statistical methods used for validation. We have developed a novel storage approach that significantly reduces the required memory by approximately two orders of magnitude, allowing us to compute three-nucleon interaction matrix elements more efficiently with accurate ab initio methods. This breakthrough enables the computation of 6He, 6He, 17O, and 42He orbits with high precision, which we then applied to obtain the ground state energy of heavy nuclei such as 6He, 6He, 17O, 42He, and 48Ca within an accurate range of 0.1 MHz. Our results demonstrate excellent agreement with experimental data on ground-state properties and accurately predict the energy spectra of these nuclei. Moreover, our calculations converge rapidly due to our novel storage approach, which in many cases enables the convergence of high-order corrections in a single computation. This advancement now makes it feasible to apply accurate ab initio methods to even heavier nuclei. Additionally, we have obtained the three-nucleon interaction coefficients of heavy nuclei, which we then used to obtain the ground-state energy and density of these nuclei through a new type of large-scale perturbation theory. Our results show that this approach converges rapidly and yields highly accurate results. Our novel storage approach also enables the computation of low-energy photo-disintegration reactions such as (e, e' de), (e, e' n), and (e, e' de) in a single calculation, which we then applied to obtain the electromagnetic form factors of 6He and 17O in agreement with experimental data. Lastly, we have utilized our novel storage approach to simulate the finite-size scaling of the chiral Lagrangian, which is crucial for obtaining precise three-nucleon interaction coefficients. Our results show that we can obtain the finite-volume energy spectrum and the first-order correction to the three-nucleon interaction coefficient without being affected by finite-volume effects. In object-oriented programming, dynamically allocating memory is crucial, yet programming this efficiently for GPUs is especially difficult because of memory access issues caused by pointer indirection.  To address this problem, we have developed a highly efficient memory allocator called DynaSOAr, specifically designed for object-oriented programming on GPUs with efficient memory access.  This innovative allocator not only ensures data structure parallelization but also optimizes memory usage by reducing memory waste, thereby maximizing memory bandwidth.  By automatically managing memory allocation for arrays of objects, DynaSOAr eliminates the need for manual memory management, significantly improving programmer productivity while efficiently utilizing the GPU's limited memory.  We have successfully integrated DynaSOAr into the OpenACC standard and demonstrated its superior performance by achieving substantial speedups and optimal memory usage in several benchmark tests.  Furthermore, we have applied DynaSOAr to real-world molecular dynamics simulations to obtain impressive memory bandwidth optimizations of up to 2.4 times, demonstrating its practical value and potential for further development.  To further expand the applicability of DynaSOAr, we have explored its generalization to support arbitrary object layouts, paving the way for a broader range of programming models and applications.  We have successfully applied this generalized approach to domain decomposition algorithms and demonstrated significant memory usage improvements of up to 2.5 times in resulting benchmark tests.  In summary, DynaSOAr offers highly efficient memory allocation solutions, significantly enhancing the performance and productivity of object-oriented programming on GPUs, with substantial potential for further innovation and development. This research develops a fully-integrated temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing voltages for the supply of digital logic. A 8-bit digital thermometer and a temperature-difference converter are designed in parallel to provide two distinct output signals, which are then combined to yield a total output signal via a differential output buffer. The resulting system achieves a temperature resolution of 0.24 degrees Celsius, a limited error margin of 1.4 degrees Celsius, and converts temperature at a rate of 1.06 nanojoules per conversion cycle. Moreover, the sensor's operating range spans from 60 to 200 degrees Celsius. This temperature sensor was successfully implemented in a 90nm CMOS process, demonstrating the benefits of minimal power consumption, compact size, and resistance to process variations. Detailed analysis and simulations validate the design's accuracy and efficiency. Experimental results from a 90nm test chip also verify the performance characteristics of the designed system. The developed temperature sensor boasts a power-efficient design that enables real-time temperature monitoring in high-performance semiconductor devices. As a result, this design offers a suitable solution for companies requiring reliable thermal monitoring in their existing voltage-range and existing CMOS processes. A summary of the temperature sensor's key features includes an output range of 0.6 to 1.8 volts, minimal power consumption of 30 femto watts, and compact chip size of 90 by 50 micrometers. Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new technique is presented to create heralded entanglement without postselection through a quantum scissors effect, which enables entangled photons to be separated and recombined at will. This innovative approach not only eliminates photon loss but also enables dynamic control of the entanglement quantity and quality. As such, it offers a significant advancement over conventional methods. We have successfully demonstrated this concept experimentally and observed high fidelity values for entangled photons, even when the fidelity is minimized. This method not only contributes to the development of free-space quantum communication networks but also paves the way for the creation of quantum memory. Consequently, it has the potential to significantly impact the field of optical quantum information processing. At its core, this method embodies an innovative application of quantum erasure, which in turn, holds significant promise for revolutionizing our understanding of entangled photons and their behavior. In essence, this research has given rise to a novel entanglement-preserving effect, which is an extraordinary finding in the realm of quantum physics. This new property, which is distinct from traditional entanglement, possesses its own set of characteristics and can be rigorously analyzed through advanced mathematical representations. One of its most striking attributes is its ability to preserve the nonlocal properties of entangled photons and maintain a constant value of the Clauser-Horne parameter, even in the absence of postselection, which in itself is a remarkable outcome. This research has successfully bridged the gap between fundamental quantum research and practical optical technologies, thereby paving the way for the development of novel optical technologies and innovations in the field of quantum information and communication. In particular, we have successfully demonstrated a new paradigm in which the concept of quantum scissors, originally described in nonlocal systems, is applied to create a heralded entanglement without postselection, which has far-reaching implications at the single-photon level. This approach offers significant advantages, particularly in terms of efficiency and performance, which has been thoroughly evaluated and shown to surpass conventional methods by an order of magnitude. As such, this study offers an innovative solution to the persistent problem of photon loss in optical quantum technologies, which has now been effectively mitigated at the single-photon level. In conclusion, this research has given rise to an entirely new set of quantum technologies

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, is tied to the properties of a specific system of special functions. The specific characteristics of this system depend on the parameters of the functions, namely, $\d$ and $\kappa$. The establishment of closed-form recurrences for functions on the sphere, ensuring positive definiteness, is essential for various statistical models of random fields. This paper presents newly derived, one-step recurrences for the invariant zonal mean of a function on the sphere, ensuring its positive definiteness. The provided recurrences generalize previously known results on the sphere and also extend the findings to functions on the plane, by employing specific parameter settings. The given recurrences facilitate the computation of a function's $n$-dimensional spectral distribution, leading to a direct relationship with a system of special functions. The provided results are further exemplified in the computation of a field's $n$-dimensional spectral mean in a Gaussian random field on the sphere, using the characteristics of a Parabolic Bessel function. The given examples showcase the applicability of the recurrences in the computation of useful field characteristics, through the exploitation of a system of special functions' properties. The provided findings can also be extended and applied in other domains, ensuring the positive definiteness of functions. A conventional imaging scenario involves sending a series of photons from an object and using an average of these photons to reconstruct the image, yet this process can be costly in terms of photons. We've developed a new method, informed by single-pixel density estimation techniques, that enables imaging with a limited number of undetected photons, thereby reducing imaging costs. This approach leverages the unique properties of quantum mechanics to eliminate unnecessary detection steps. We've successfully implemented the method using a 64-pixel square pixel array and have demonstrated its capability to perform high-resolution imaging at a low cost by working with a limited number of undetected photons. Furthermore, we have quantified the optimal balance between resolution and image quality by determining the critical density of states for the object's photons. We have successfully demonstrated the method's ability to perform clear images of a dollar bill using 10 million undetected photons and 2 million detected photons for reconstruction. We have also utilized the method to create a real-time video of a moving object using 40 million undetected photons and 8 million detected photons for reconstruction. These results have successfully demonstrated a quantum imaging protocol that utilizes single-pixel techniques and interacts freely with the object to achieve high-quality images at a low cost. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. We have provided a comprehensive classification of the different friction modes and have suggested a new "unpinned bubble" regime that emerges during the transition from the stick-slip to the stationary regime. The transition from the stick-slip to the stationary regime is accompanied by a significant and sudden change in stress, suggesting a switch from an unpinned to a pinned state of the bubbles within the foam. The persistence of surface slippage is primarily influenced by the distribution of stress among the liquid and gas phases. While this phenomenon may initially seem analogous to dry friction in solids, our data also reveal subtle differences driven by the presence of a liquid phase. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the complex interplay between surface roughness, liquid-gas mixtures, and the dynamics of dry foams, and successfully bridges the gap between this context and the study of nanoparticle-based tribology. Additionally, this work may contribute to the development of novel, surfactant-free materials with tailored friction properties. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 12 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating metadata into image analysis enhances classification accuracy across all tasks. Notably, our methods successfully detected the outlier class with high accuracy, and when ensemble voting from the 12 CNN classifiers is used, a classification accuracy of 93.9% was achieved across all tasks. With a binary classification of the anomalous class, an accuracy of 97.3% was achieved by integrating a entropy-based classifier alongside the ensemble vote. A combination of our methods with a entropy-based approach to classify the anomalous class and a supervised classifier for task 2 yielded an accuracy of 94.8%. Furthermore, our findings indicate that incorporating metadata increased the accuracy of classes with rare skin conditions, such as melanoma, seborrhoic keratosis, and pseudocarcinoma. Our work also discovered a metadata-based approach to classify images into healthy or diseased, achieving high accuracy across all tasks. We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from earlier research. These findings amplify the need for theoretical models more advanced than the random phase approximation. Contrary to the hypothesis suggesting significant acceleration of the carriers due to their interaction with spin fluctuations, our results do not support this theory. Additionally, a comparison with previous electron loss data indicates that sodium's mass enhancement due to dipole-type electron-hole interactions is substantially less than its mass enhancement due to monopole-type interactions measured using ARPES. Based on these outcomes, we suggest that sodium's mass enhancement is entirely caused by dipole-type interactions, and a subsequent relaxation process. We also validated the hyperbolic momentum dependence of the lifetime of quasi-particles in sodium, determined the magnitude of its density-of-states, and calculated the strength of electron-hole interaction within this strength. These findings were then compared with numerical simulations, and we observed agreement between the results from both ARPES and electron loss experiments. Furthermore, we determined that a finite lifetime of quasi-particles in sodium exists over a momentum range of at least 0.065 π /a, which is significantly larger than previously estimated. Our study demonstrates the capabilities of synchrotron-based ARPES in examining the complex behavior of nearly-free electron metals while also highlighting the need for more sophisticated theoretical models. High-resolution images from the SOLIS project reveal tiny magnetic bright points across the solar surface, indicating extremely strong magnetic fields. These features, detected in all solar layers, appear as small bright points, roughly 100-200 km in size, emitting electromagnetic radiation in the chromosphere and outer photosphere. To better understand their characteristics, we analyzed images of magnetic bright points in the continuum and Ca II 393.37 nm bands, using a Gaussian distribution model to fit their distributions. This model separates the points into two components with distinct sizes, ranging from small (~110 km) to large (~220 km), and separates them spatially. We found that the smaller bright points are predominantly a lower layer phenomenon, appearing in photospheric images but not in continuum images of the chromosphere, whereas the larger bright points are prevalent in all images. These results suggest that the smaller bright points are generated by magnetic interactions at the boundary of convection zones, while the larger ones are related to magnetic torsion in the convective zone that penetrates into the chromosphere. This two-component model provides a better fit than a single distribution model, confirming our findings with different data sets and solarscales. However, we found that the size distribution of magnetic bright points does not depend on their area, location, or temperature. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of small magnetic bright points that can help explain their role in redistributing magnetic flux across the solar surface. We propose that the efficient transport of magnetic flux through the convective zone is primarily due to the penetration of large magnetic bright points, while the small ones are confined at the boundary of the convective zone. Moreover, we found that the area of magnetic bright points in the photosphere is correlated with their radiance, but this correlation disappears at higher altitudes. This study also shows that the distribution of magnetic bright points in the Ca II 393.37 nm band is larger than in the photosphere and near-continuum images, indicating that their growth is triggered by magnetic field force loops in the chromosphere. We found that about 50% of magnetic bright points in the chromosphere are also present in the photosphere, demonstrating that their lifespan in the chromosphere is comparable to their residence time in the photosphere. Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in reduced modalities, such as spatial alone or minimal video. Conversely, advanced deep networks struggle with dynamic scene understanding when provided only a minimal video, necessitating both spatial and temporal input. This discrepancy suggests that current deep networks may not replicate the human visual system's processing capabilities. To bridge this gap, we created a new minimal video dataset, called MoCoObjects, comprising 10 new object categories that are distinct from existing datasets. This new set includes synchronized camera views and objects moving along varied trajectories, offering greater diversity in motion patterns. The MoCoObjects dataset comprises 1,440 videos across 120 categories and is designed to mimic real-world object movements. It includes views of objects interacting with each other, emulating common scenarios in vision datasets. The dataset's breadth of motion patterns and interactive object views provide a more comprehensive representation of dynamic scene recognition. As a result, advanced deep networks are required to perform even more complex computations to recognize the objects, making them less efficient than human vision. Ultimately, this study presents a new benchmark for dynamic scene recognition and a more accurate model of visual processing, prompting further research into the development of more biologically plausible computer vision algorithms. The new minimal video dataset, MoCoObjects, is accessible at the following link: https://moco-objects.github.io/. Dark particles interacting through Abelian gauge symmetries and ordinary matter through kinetic mixing can take the form of either magnetic monopoles or photons. By assuming that the dark sector's magnetic field is generated solely by the motion of dark monopoles, we model the dark particles as objects with an intrinsic magnetic charge similar to 't Hooft polynomials and apply this to a specific galaxy. Due to the strong magnetic fields, the dark monopoles' motion is severely restricted, resulting in a significantly reduced rate of galactic magnetic field loss compared to previous predictions. Furthermore, we find that the required milli-mono mass is within the reach of current and future particle colliders. The study's findings are then extended to investigate the stability of dark matter, with the possibility of testing our hypothesis with astrophysical observations of galactic magnetic fields over the next decade. If observations over this period show a significant decrease, it would support our model as a valid explanation for dark matter stability. However, if no decrease is observed, it may indicate the presence of additional dark sectors or a more complex dark matter scenario in which the dark current is not linked to galactic magnetic fields. Additionally, we find that the required milli-mono mass is significantly higher than the reach of LHC for a dark current of 10^-18, but still within the reach of future HLLHC for a dark current of 10^-19. In this case, we predict that the dark current will reach a minimum value of around 10^-20 by the time LHC reach is matched by other particle colliders. Lastly, we explore the possibility of directly detecting these milli-magnetic monopoles using highly sensitive detectors, resulting in an expected detection rate of around 1-10 predicted detections per year based on current detector limits and a dark monopole cross-section two orders of magnitude smaller than the standard magnetic monopole value. However, we also find that the dark monopoles could potentially be captured and stored in magnetic traps on Earth, allowing for a significantly extended storage time of around 100 years and a greatly increased detection rate of around 10,000 detections per year. In this capture and storage scenario, we predict that the required milli-mono mass would be outside the reach of LHC and would likely be outside the reach of future HLLHC unless the dark current is significantly modified by additional interactions not present in the standard model. Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with parameters $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ where $\alpha$ ranges between $0$ and $1$ and $\beta$ is restricted to $0 \leq \beta \leq 1-\alpha$. These models can be seen as variations of the Jaccard distance and are connected to an analogue of the Shannon information distance, specifically the normalized Hamming distance, for $\alpha=\frac{1}{n}$ and $\beta=1-\frac{1}{n}$. In this note, we present the general formula for $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ and prove that it is indeed a metric on the complete universe with elements $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. Furthermore, we show that the Shannon information distance is a specific case of $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ and establish its relationship with the Jaccard distance. Additionally, we provide a formula for calculating the distance between two subsets of any complete universe with elements $\{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k\}$ and derive a convenient method for computing the distance between two integers. Finally, we present experimental results demonstrating that the number of distinct elements in our universe is a low-degree polynomial in $n$ for $\alpha=\frac{1}{n}$ and $\beta=1-\frac{1}{n}$ as $n$ approaches infinity. This value of the polynomial allows us to verify that our previous analytical results for the Jaccard distance are equivalent to the known results in the literature. Our study connects the Shannon information distance with the Jaccard distance and establishes their relationship under a shared metric, $S_{\frac{1}{n},1-\frac{1}{n}}$. This connection allows us to broaden the applicability of the Shannon information distance to sets that are not equiprobable. Moreover, our results showcase an analogy between the universe's elements and the digits of the binary representation of integers, where the distance metric, $S_{\frac{1}{n},1-\frac{1}{n}}$, can be seen as a combination of the Hamming distance and the factorization distance. Ultimately, our study provides a unified understanding of the Jaccard distance and the Shannon information distance through our general metric, $S_{\alpha,\beta}$. Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired frames outside of a blurring influence to train a deblurring network.  Although paired data is challenging and expensive to obtain, many existing methods rely heavily on such data.  In response, this study develops an innovative approach by incorporating a pseudo-blur synthesizer to generate artificial blur from clear images, eliminating the need for paired data.  By doing so, training can utilize a diverse set of images under a blurring influence without requiring corresponding clear frames.  Furthermore, the proposed method also addresses the issue of low frequency preservation that is often neglected in existing methods.  As a result, it demonstrates better performance in a variety of applications, including deblurring of images, videos, and surveillance footage, as well as restoration of motion hazy images.  Our method also shows superior performance in a field that is complementary to its capabilities, specifically, image de-noising.  Ultimately, the method's efficiency and effectiveness are confirmed through evaluations using a custom database of artificially blurred images and other widely used datasets.  The study's source code is available on GitHub at the link provided.  Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in image and video deblurring as well as motion dehazing.  In particular, it demonstrates superior performance in dealing with complex and challenging scenarios such as blurs similar to camera noise, blurs with a fixed pattern, and blurs combined with low resolution and noise.  In the case of video deblurring, the method also shows superior performance in restoring the original video quality from a blurred video.  In addition to video deblurring, the method has been shown to improve the clarity of images that become hazy due to motion in images.  In general, the method's effectiveness and efficiency are attributed to its innovative approach of artificial blur synthesis and its ability to improve image and video quality through more accurate blurring removal.  In the case of low frequency preservation, the method uses a separate network to maintain the original low frequency information, resulting in more natural and clear images and videos.  In terms of the method's value, its use of artificial blur synthesis allows for image and video deblurring without paired data, resulting in faster training times.  In contrast, existing methods based on paired data require more images to be collected and paired, resulting in longer training times.  In terms of the method's reliability, its use of low frequency preservation allows for more natural and clear images and videos

The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of the set itself by taking into account infinite sequences of elements from it. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered sets. It turns out that a set is complete, meaning it contains all its upper bounds, in the resulting ultrapower if and only if it has a certain property: every group of sequences that have a common upper bound within the set also has a common upper bound within the set itself. In a way, this property can be seen as a measure of the set's completeness. As a result of this relationship, a set that is complete is always a substructure of its ultrapower, meaning it contains all the necessary information to describe the structure of its ultrapower. Moreover, a set's completeness determines whether the ultrapower is a complete set, meaning it contains all its upper bounds. If a set is complete, then the ultrapower as a refined version of the set itself is also complete. Conversely, this indicates that a set that is not complete does not influence whether its refined version as an ultrapower is complete or not. In a way, this can be seen as a measure of a set's completeness as a fundamental property of its structure. Notably, this also implies that a CPT-based solution for the halting problem of Turing machines, derived from a prior result, is both feasible and inevitable. Many software systems offer comprehensive configuration settings that enable users to tailor the program to their needs, often resulting in an enormous space of possible settings.  In this space, a specific subset of settings that deliver optimal performance or quality is typically of greatest interest, although finding it efficiently may not always be practical or desirable.  If the optimal configuration is consistently required in every execution, setting it at run-time can be a costly process, especially if the cost is high relative to the execution time.  To address this challenge, we propose a new framework that enables a substantial reduction in the configuration space under the assumption that there are distinct optimal settings for specific user needs.  Our approach involves classifying these needs at run-time and leveraging this information to determine the relevant attributes at compile-time.  We evaluate this concept on three real-world systems, demonstrating that it can substantially minimize the configuration space and also predict the optimal configuration with confidence.  We validate the accuracy of our model in a controlled environment, verifying that the predicted configurations match the ones identified through manual evaluation.  Furthermore, we show that the proposed framework reduces the configuration space by an average of two orders of magnitude without incurring any run-time overhead.  Our experience with this framework suggests that its success depends on the quality of the code and the relevance of the attributes being modified through the configuration settings.  We identify several areas for further improvement and invite the research community to build upon our work, exploring new directions such as partially specialized configurations or developing more sophisticated learning techniques.  Ultimately, we believe that our study opens up new avenues for efficient configuration management in software development. We evaluate this approach on two tasks: part-of-speech tagging and dependency parsing, and successfully apply it across three language pairs: English-French, English-Spanish, and French-Spanish. The results show significant improvements in accuracy for all three pairs, with gains of up to 14.90% in our experiments. Furthermore, our model outperforms state-of-the-art multilingual models in POS tagging and dependency parsing on the CoNLL2003 and UD Treebank datasets. We also explore using our task representations as weak supervision for semantic role labeling and achieve notable gains of up to 4.10% in our experiments. These results indicate that neural task representations can serve as an effective model-independent tool for multilingual applications. They also have potential to be used as a form of weak supervision for other NLP tasks, offering a cost-effective and data-efficient approach to enhancing model performance. In multi-task reinforcement learning, agents learn a variety of skills by adapting to different scenarios.  Despite the effectiveness of model-based approaches in learning these skills, they often struggle with a lack of clarity when deciding which past experience to use and how to apply it to the current situation.  This ambiguity can lead to excessive variability in experience selection, causing the agent to experience a high level of noise and poor performance.  However, we discover that using modular networks to represent experiences can reduce this noise and result in more stable learning outcomes.  By organizing experience into separate categories, agents can focus on absorbing the key information in each setting, leading to clearer connections between cause and effect and significantly improved performance in learning multiple skills.  This approach is particularly beneficial in challenging scenarios, such as navigation and physics-based games, and can be easily adapted for use in self-supervised learning without the guidance of rewards.  By applying this strategy, agents can learn a range of useful skills across a variety of tasks and achieve superior results.  Additionally, the knowledge gained from these skills can be transferred to new tasks, demonstrating a strong generalization ability in the learned models. Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity.  Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for identifying these planets.  In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar activity by analyzing solar data collected by the HARPS-N instrument on the GTC telescope.  Using a machine learning algorithm, we identified patterns in the solar spectrum that are linked to various features of stellar activity.  Our findings indicate that the most reliable indicators are connected to variations in the star's rotation.  In contrast, the spectral patterns of the star's vibrations have little predictive value for these planetary phenomena.  We discovered that using activity indicators alone is insufficient to accurately predict sunspot indices, as other factors influence these indicators as well.  Nevertheless, our study suggests that these activity indicators can help in the detection of Earth-like exoplanets.  Additionally, we found that using spectral features alone is insufficient to accurately classify the star's level of activity and that other characteristics must be considered.  Finally, we determined that using the spectral features of Ca II is superior to using other features for identifying active regions on the star, particularly for partial coverage where other indicators fall short.  Using simulated data, we found that using these spectral features can help detect sub-jovian exoplanets with an accuracy of 0.6-0.7.  However, further investigation is needed to validate this method.  In particular, we propose that using a combination of spectral features and light curves can significantly improve our ability to accurately detect planetary signals.  Therefore, combining photometric and spectroscopic data is essential for accurately identifying exoplanets, particularly those with longer periods. Event identification is crucial for understanding evolving phenomena such as spreading diseases and popular social trends.  Unlike situations with fixed structures, event detection on graphs that change over time is a challenging problem.  Most current methods construct a single unified graph from all time slices and employ a traditional graph mining framework, which leads to overly broad event definitions.  To address this issue, a new framework called EDG is proposed that leverages a node-based approach and defines events based on significant clusterings in graph snapshots at different time points.  Each event corresponds to a cluster of strongly connected components in a graph snapshot, and its significance is measured by the number of nodes within the cluster.  To effectively identify these clusters, a new algorithm is developed that combines a streaming component graph format and a memory-efficient linear programming (LP) optimization framework.  To combat the computational complexity of the LP algorithm, a corresponding streaming algorithm is also developed that iterates the construction of a forest from the graph snapshot and optimizes node groupings through analysis of node forward and backward paths.  This algorithm iteratively updates forest structures and evaluates the best LP objective as new edges are added in a streaming component graph format, and when a predetermined number of iterations is reached, the algorithm reverts to a traditional component graph format and the forest structures are discarded.  Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms traditional methods in accurately detecting events and evaluating their significance.  Additionally, the framework shows promising applications in real-world scenarios such as coauthor analysis and social network event detection.  A comprehensive study on the dataset $\text{NYP}^{+}$ reveals that $\text{NYP}^{+}_{\text{EDG}}$ achieves superior performance compared to $\text{NYP}^{+}_{\text{Mod1}}$ and $\text{NYP}^{+}_{\text{Mod2}}$ in terms of precision, recall, and F1-score.  Another real-world dataset $\text{MSL}^{+}$ is analyzed using the proposed framework, and the resulting graphs from node-based approaches are compared visually to images from Google Maps and Street View.  The analysis indicates that the framework successfully detects meaningful events related to event types 'crime' and 'disorder', and the resulting graphs from node-based approaches match the visual content from these other sources.  The proposed framework demonstrates promising performance in event detection and analysis on real-world datasets and outperforms traditional methods in accuracy and visual representations. The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and the ability for people to understand the decisions made by these systems will become increasingly crucial, prompting a greater demand for the explanations they provide. We propose a two-fold approach in response to this need. Firstly, we will define the key characteristics of explainable AI as it relates to human understanding. Secondly, we will develop a framework for capturing the requirements surrounding the explanations of AI systems, taking into account the diverse nature of stakeholders and their varying needs. By doing so, we aim to establish a foundation for integrating explainability into AI development, thereby improving trust and acceptance among users. Our aim is to demonstrate how Requirements Engineering can play a pivotal role in shaping the future of AI, ultimately serving as a model for other complex technological systems. We will illustrate our approach using the example of a medical AI system, and then evaluate its applicability to a diverse set of AI applications across various domains, including the social sector, industry, and the military. Finally, we will identify promising avenues for further research and highlight potential short-term outcomes, in addition to the long-term potential for creating more transparent and understandable AI systems. Our ultimate goal is to foster a more collaborative relationship between Requirements Engineering and AI research, leading to the development of more user-centric AI applications. We advocate for the integration of Requirements Engineering as a vital component in creating and implementing AI systems that are truly tailored to human needs. By doing so, we can increase the system's explainability and improve the explanations provided to stakeholders, ultimately resulting in enhanced system functionality and greater acceptance among users. Essential requirements for achieving this goal include establishing a shared understanding of key terms and developing a unified framework for capturing and prioritizing AI explainability requirements. Our proposed approach marks a significant long-term achievement in this endeavor, enabling the creation of more transparent and understandable AI systems through the integration of Requirements Engineering as a vital component. We can improve the explanations provided to stakeholders and increase system functionality by prioritizing user needs, thereby earning greater acceptance among users. Essential to this process is a shared understanding of key terms and a unified framework for capturing and prioritizing AI explainability requirements. We illustrate our proposed approach using concrete examples from diverse domains, including the social sector (e.g., mental health), industry (e.g., product recommendations), and the military (e.g., predictive analytics for gunfire detection). Accurate diagnosis and management of colorectal polyps heavily rely on the examination of histological slides, which are then supplemented by whole-slide imaging (WSI). To enhance digital pathology research and improve patient outcomes, we developed UniToPatho, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 1,226 histological slides from 312 patients with annotated labels indicating the type of colorectal lesion, along with adenoma grading levels. This dataset is specifically tailored for the UniTo of Padova Hospital's specimens. We meticulously assessed the characteristics of UniToPatho and utilized it to train various convolutional neural network models for classification and regression tasks. Our findings indicate that, in comparison to alternative methods, a pre-trained SeNet-based model achieved the best results for classification, accuracy, and correlation, ultimately demonstrating a strong potential for the widespread adoption of deep learning-based systems in the classification of colorectal lesions. Conversely, a combination of features from different images outperformed a model trained with a SeNet-based method in predicting dysplasia grades. Consequently, we believe that UniToPatho can serve as a valuable resource for researchers engaged in the development of advanced computer-assisted diagnostic tools to streamline the colorectal polyps classification and adenoma grading process. This dataset is accessible at https://github.com/hieundoan/UntoPatho.git. It is also expected to be uploaded to https://clic.adoc.institut-imager.fr/. In addition, the code used in this study will be shared on https://github.com/hieundoan/UntoPatho.git.

A novel method called MrSARP combines a hierarchical generative model with an automatic relevance determination regulator to leverage a trained deep neural network as a prior for under-sampling in synthetic aperture radar (SAR) image generation.  As a low-frequency component generator, MrSARP utilizes a pre-trained neural network to generate coarse-resolution images, while a high-frequency component generator employs the regulator to guide a neural network as a prior for high-frequency details in the SAR image generation process.  Experimental evaluations confirm that MrSARP produces superior-quality SAR images with relevant high-frequency components and achieves notable performance improvements over existing methods within the under-sampling framework.  Additionally, MrSARP exhibits a strong capacity to generalize to new SAR datasets, producing image quality that rivals that of datasets specifically used in its training.
